"Then, gracious lady," said a German baron to a lady- to whom he had made an offer of marriage, "am I to understand that you reject my offer? In that case I have only one request to make, which I fervently hope you will not refuse." Young lady: "What is it 7" Herr baron: "That you will never, never betray what I have just revealed to you of the deep feelings or my most in- most heart." Young lady: "Oh, certainly not I But I why?' Herr baron; "Because—ahem i—well—because ' I intend proposing to your elder sister to-morrow." I Learn to govern ourselves, and to be genial and patient. • Guard your tempers, especially in seasons of ill-health, irritation, and trouble, and soften them by prayers, and a sense of your own shortcomings and errors. Remem- ber that, valuable as is the gift of speech, silence is often t much more valuable. Do not expect too much from others. Never retort a sharp or angry word. It is the I second word that makes the quarrel_ Do not examine too minutely the actions of your friends, nor the motives , which actuated them. If they have acted with a want I of delicacy, appear not to understand it; or, what is more simple, think that it was a mistake on their part. The Roman Catholic clergyman of a town in a Midland • county is a native of the Emerald Isle, and, like many of his countrymen, a great humourist, while nobody en- joys a joke better. He is familiarly known by the title of Father M., and is on friendly terms with the clergy- 'men of the other denominations in the neighbourhood. At a school bard election the clergyman of the parish church, on entering the polling-booth to 'record his vote, met Father M. coming out, and saluted him with "Oh, your reverence, what are you doing here?" Father M., who had jnst deposited his voting paper in the ballot-. box, replied, with a merry twinkle in his eyes, "This Is no place for confession !" A porter at a Scottish railway station, who had grown gray in the service, was one day superintending matters on the platform, when the wash minister stepped up to him and asked when the next train arrived from the south. The aged official took off his cap and carefully read the hour and the minute of the train from a docu- ment stuck in the crown. Somewhat surprised at this, the minister said—" Dear me, John, is your memory ;failing, or what is up with you? You used to have all these matters entirely by heart." " Weel, sir," said John, (" I dinna ken if my memory's Min' or fat's up; but the fac' is, I'm just growin' like yerser—l canna manage without the paper.". HIS Warn= n Goan.—A curious ceremony was-per- ,• formed the other day at Travancore. The Maharajah I was weighed against a mass of pure gold, which was then dispensed in charity. This custom, called " Tulabhara," is one of great antiquity, and is said to be traceable in Travancore to the fourth century. It is not unknown in other parts of India; though, of course, gold is only used in the case of wealthy persons, the humbler sort , being content to weigh themselves against -spices or , grain. On the present occasion the Maharajah weighed a I little over nine stone. The Brahmins, it is said, wished to defer the ceremony, in the hope that the Maharajah might more nearly approachlthe weight of his father, I who did not undergo the rite until 47 years old, when he j weighed 144 stone. A good many years ago there lived in Barbadoes a General Haynes, whose state garb included a puce or ,claret-coloured coat. He was a well-known and much- respected character:. A Barbadian planter came to ' England about that time, and, as is usual with new arrivals, desired a fresh " rig-out," and with this view he betook himself, when in London, to a West End tailor. See with orient beam yon desert sun Like fire of some great furnace, slowly rise %Climbing the sky; from whence, his fiery throne, He fills the earth with light, and darkness flies. As morning breaks apace the growing dawn reveals The hurried camp, where, wearied out, the tired soldiers seek A fitful slumber, dreaming there, perchance of. distant

fields And meadows green, or herues:remote upon the - moorland Weak. _ The day wears on, they see the sullen foe Gathered to bar their passage to the Nile, Advance they must; their burning thirst can know No respite, till,they've made the desperate trial. And hark! What sound is this which rings out to tho air With clear and strident note; it is the bugle call! Quick to your r tnks, lads—and with weapons bare Shoulder to shoulder wait the storm now threatening one and all.

Like torrent burst from bed of Alpine stream, Which rushes madly down in headlong course, Like crash of silver-crested wave with lightning gleam, Washed on the storm-beat coast with thundering force. So on the silent ranks of England's martial sons Breaks the fierce chivalry of Arab war, With hideous clamours rising,. I Tom their lungs,
To urge each other forward—on they pour.' But all in vain against that steadfast band; No force of theirs can break that line of steel; But backward borne and scattered like the sand

The desert host in dire:confusion reel. But e'er they turn, somd:randorn bullet sped From unknown hand, has wrought a woful deed. Our leader falls; his noble life by noblest spirit led Ebbs fast away, a ransom to his country's need. His soldiers gather round with deep and bitter grief! Tenderly they raise and bear him 'cross the burning sand. No arms but theirs shall do this-work—their hearts ask no relief Until he's laid for ever in that far and lonely land. All honour to thee, gallant Stewart, beside thy bloody bier • A nation mourns in speechless grief a soldier tried and true; A stainless life, a gentle life, a soil that knew not fear, ' Ideal type of British race, thy loss we long shall rue. The memory of thy gallant death will live for evermore As to our sons in years to come the stirring tale we'll tell, And men will talk throughout the land in homes of rich and poor Of him who sleeps a soldier's sleep beside the Gakdul Well. —London Society.

A lawyer could not act for both plaintiff and defendant, and it did not in this ease look well for the same medical officer to have both duties. Therefore he could not see sufficient reason for taking these people beck to the Workhouse. Had the school never been built, they would have had the boys at the House, and they would not have thought it incom- patible with the duties of Dr. Spinks for him to attend the adult bays as well as the children. He was certain Mr. Henley did not suggest such a thing as their haying a eeparate medical man for the school, and he did not thiuk that they should deprive Dr. Spinks of a portion of the eraoluments he received as medical officer of the House. There did seem a shadow of injustice about it, and he did not see how it would in any way tend to mitigate what had taken place in the school.—Mr. Herm endorsed the remarks of Mr. Harrison.—Mr. APPLETON supported the amend- ment. Dr. Spinks, he pointed out, had been medical officer for over 30 years, and it would almost be strange did not an oversight or mistake occur in that long period. He thought that to pass the resolution would indeed be dealing harshly with Dr. Spinks, who, he thought, deserved a little more consideration at their hands. He aloo considered that it was in the discretion of the Board to send paupers to the school, if they could use their services without injury. They were not dressed as paupers, and there was no appearance of pauperism in their ban.. there. He thought they might use a little of their own discretion in that matter. They were not servants of Mr. Henley, but Guardians, and they were not bound to do what Mr. Henley said Inspectors were only officials.eent there to report, and Guardians had a little discretion left them after they (the inspectors) had been. They pail the money, and gave their services, and he thought that as members of the Board they were more important than was Mr. Henley. (A. voice : Certainly we ate.) He should support the amenclmene—Mr. FOSTER supported the original resolution. As regarded the removal of the paupers Ins did not think they should set up their discretion against that of the Inspector. He thought that was a little more even than Mr. Appleton, in hie valiant spirit, would care to do. 'The committee came to the conclusicn, after what Mr. Henley had said, that to introduce paupers at all at Padgate School was to violate the principles for which the school was established. If there were only one pauper there the principle was broken, and the Inspector said that they were doing wrong. Ile thought the gentlemen who were opposing the minutes were making rather too personal a matter of the recommendation regarding the medical officer. It was not so as far as the committee were con- cerned, their principle being that it was not desirable for obis man to act for both places. Tbatopinion had been formed tie- fore, and over-ridden by the Beard, and now gentlemen who bad rot discussed the matter with the committee were seeking to over-ride a similar recommendation that came to the Board backed up by the suggestions and experience of Mr. Eienley.—Mr. DABBILSHIRII spoke in favour of the minutes. He pointed out that by the present arrangement one medical officer was given jurisdiction in another's district. He thought it inconsistent that in a neighbourhood where they had a medical officer there should be one house over which another medical officer had charge. kr. GREENING thotight it would be better if they could do without paupers at the school. There were cases, perhaps, where it was pos- sible that paupers who had been employed, might bertha- charged and then re-engaged, but not as paupers, if they were suitable people. Ho thought it was repeat credit to Dr. Spinks to have held his position for 30 sears, and that he must have fulfilled his duties well, but on the other band he thought it better that they should have two medical officiere.—Mr. iliaresme suggested that Mr. Henley, with the zeal that always accompanied a newly appointed officer, might have formeda more serious view of the matter than I perhaps his predecessors might have done.—Mr. BROAD- BENT believed that Mr. Henley was one of the oldest and most experienced officers of "that department. (A voice: Yes.) He added that the wish of the committee was to make the schools among the best managed in the country. Every member who had spoken in opposition had dwelt upon the consideration that they should show to the medical officer and certain other individuals, but not one had said a word about the consideration they should pay to the chil- dren. (Hear. hear.) Mr.. Wood, of Chapeldonin, has been trying the ex- periment of growing potatoes by the use of artificinl .mailores alone. He has for over a dozen consecutive. years, grown potatoes on the same land without any ap- plication of farmyaid manure, which is contrary to or- i dmary customs and ideas. In the main, the results have ' "beia tavoufalle. - . The total number of animals Imported from all sources in 1884 was 3,099,719, against 3,103,495 in 1883. Qf that number 715,843 e,attle; 633,285 sheep,- and 456,678 swine were received from Ireland. Of the 3,114 cargoes of animals landed in Great Britain from places out of the United Kingdom, 23 cargoes were reported to be diseased; 17 of these were from the United States. ..

Mr. John H. M'Culloch, of Melbourne who was well- known several years ago in Galloway, sails for Melbourne in a few days with a well-assorted lot of Clydesdale horses. Amongst them are Caledonia (3449),' and the famous prize stallion Sir Michael (1530). Mr. M'Cialloch. also takes out Lord Kenmuir (4181), bred by Mr. Spittal, Kenmuir. This horse is a grandson of Prince of Wales 073), and is a very promising young horse. -- Ting UNDERLEY HER.D.—In the herd of the Earl opee- tive the following births have occurred :—April sth, Darlington 26th, roan c C; April 7th, Underley Darling Bth, white bC; April 11th, Gwynneth 2nd, roan b c; April 12th, Baroness Waterloo, white b c; AprillBth, Red Rose of Nittsdale, b c, all by Grand Duke 31st, 38,374; April 21st, Fairydalo, red and white c c (dead), by Lord Solway; April 21st, Darlington Duchess 7th, roan c ç by Grand Duke 31st, 38,374. ERADICATING Ittisrins.—The most effectual method of eradicating rushes is by thoroughly draining the land, and applying afterwards a heavy dressing of lime or chalk on the spots where the rushes abound. Lime should be put on in the early spring, and chalk in .the autumn or winter, so that it might be pulverised by frost. The rushes should not be allowed to make much growth at any time, but should be kept cut down, which weakens them and prevents their development.— SavEni.r. FOOD OF7THE Sow.—lt IS difficult to appreciate how much is required of the saw in rearing her litter, espe- cially if it be a large one. It has been estimated that with eight pigs the sow will be called on for about 10Ib. of milk per day for the first week, Mb. for the second, and 201 b. for the third. To furnish this enormous supply the best of food and care is needed, and where skim- milk and other food can be substituted for the brood, this should also be done, in order tol lessen the drain upon the sow as much as possible. The milk of the sow, however, being the most nourishing food the young pigs can have, it is well to so feed her that she may be able to supply as much food for them as possible. SALE OF PURE-BRED STOCK.—A ,few 'days Ilago, the Hindlip herd of Sir Henry Allsopp, of Hindlip Hall, was dispersed by Mr. Thornton. About I,soo:persons assem- bled round the ring including Earl Bective. and Earl Lathom. Mr. Thornton referred atAha outset ta the choice breeding and high character of the stock, remark- ing that with much public benefit Sir Henry Allsopp had devoted part of his life to the breeding of high-class stock. Whether of horses, cattle, or sheep, the best only were brought to Hindlip. He- regretted that the herd had to dome into the market- at such an unfavourable time as the present; and in speaking of the merit of the herd, mentioned that last year Sir Henry Allsopp realised no less than £4,000 for his bulls. He was:sure the com- pany would appreciate the excellent arrangements which Mr. Riddell and others had made for their ,comfort, and .e hoped they would enable him to make to Sir Henry Allsopp an adequate return for his valuable cattle.—We add a summary of the averages for tribes : Average. Duchess, 9 cows and heifers £362 2 9} 2693 0 0 „ 6 bulls 15 animals 2T/ 19 5 Oxford, 5 cows and heifers „ 2 bulls 126 10 6 8 animals Red Bose, 17 covis and heifers Bl 19 1 „ 3 bulls ........ ............. 84 0 0 20 anhuals B2 3 3 Waterloo, 3 cows and heifers l6B 7 • 0 „ 2 bulls 5 animals llB 0 5 BUTTER AND IMITATIONS: ITS TEST.—It is pretty we'V known that there is as yet no absolutely perfect chemi- cal test by which butter can be distinguished from imita- tions, although it is admitted that there is a considerable difference between the melting point of the one and the other. From America comes a plain and practical test whiCh is stated to have been adopted by a butterman. The person in question when requested appears to be quite willing to convince his customers that the article he sells as butter is genuine if they desire it. He always has near at hand two small receptacles with% quantity of lamp-wick in each, and when he wishes to make the test he places a portion of butter and oleomargarine into two separate cups or tin mugs. These he heats until the contents are thoroughly melted, when the butter is poured into one of the first-named =receptacles and the oleomargarine into the other. The wicks are now lighted, and in a very short space of time two quite distinct odours may be recigniscd, one of which, that from the butter, is pleasant and agreeable to the smell, while the other, being that from the oleomargarine, is obnoxious to a high degree. He is delighted with the discovery he has made, and he has an especial reason to be so if, as he states, his business has in consequence doubled in ex- tent.

SKIM-MILK CHEESE.—" A Correspondent" asked for in- structions for .making skim-milk cheese. A Gloucester dairywonaan to -whom was sent his question gives the following rules for making thin cheese—" either skim or best :"—Put the rennet into milk at 85deg., stir it well, and cover it over for an hour or nearly. Then gently break with curd-breaker. When about half broken, let it rest a few minutes; then dip off gently some of the whey into a warmer, and, when heated, return it to the

, cheese-tub, breaking the „ curd till quite smalL The temperature should now be not lower than 87deg., and in cold weather 90deg. If necessary, more whey must be heated. Now cover, and leave it to settle for half an _ _

hour; then draw together, and drain off the whey. Place the curd in vats, and press for half an hour; then return it to cheese-tub, grind, and let it cooL Place carefully in vats, and return to the press. In an hour put on dry cloths; two hours later salt the cheeses on both sides. On the two next mornings again salt the cheeses in the cloths, and the following morning salt again and return to bare vats. The next day they may be removed, and placed on boards to dry. Weight of curd from 100 gallons of skim-milk, about 661bs. after June In the spring the milk produces less. Honss TAmixo.—On Saturday afternoon, Professor Hamilton Sample, of America, .assisted by Professor Galvayne, inaugurated at Hengler's Circus a class for instruction in his system of taming and training young or vicious horses. Professor Sample explained that his mode of procedure was not only based upon horse nature, but was perfectly humane, a remark which he supported by producing a testimonial from the Melbourne Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. Many mis- takes were made in the management of horses. Some people looked upon them as very intelligent, but if they, had anything like the intelligence with which they were credited, they would kick the heads clean off half thel men who undertook to manage them. (Laughter.) The Professor went On to contend, with the help of:an anec- dote, that horses ought not to be kept awayfrom things that frightened them, but should be made familiar with them till their alarm died away. It was very often believed that the horse was submissive to manfiecause

- ---- • - its eye magnified its master to seven times his: natural size. If that were true the animal when about to bite a carrot two inches in diameter would'!" open its mouth to a width of fourteen inches—(laughter)--and everybody knew that that was not the case.—Profedsor Galvayne described what he had himself done recently at York, Thirsk, and elsewhere by his colleague's sys- tem. Persons who had seen the result of:their work without knowing how it had been brought about ac- cused them of using drugs, but the pupils whom they expected to receive in London would see that the charge was quite untrue. After the speeches several horses were brought into the ring. The first had been sent by a London gentleman to be operated upon as unmanage- able, but when mounted by an Australian rough rider, who accompanies Professor Sample, it seemed quite docile. Three others which had been under the pro- fessor's treatment once each were perfectly submissive, one of them, described as a three-year-old thorough- bred, running round the ring with a pole between its legs and with tin cans tied to its tail. It also stood still, though evidently nervous, while some crackers went off near its heels. • Finally, an unbroken colt was brought in, and in two or three minutes patiently sub- mitted to having an umbrella opened and shut rapidly over its head, although at first the mere sight of the machine startled it.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

POTATOES.—The earliest of these are now through the ground, and will need earthing up in order to protect them from frost, a few degrees of which destroys them to the ground level. When this occurs the parent tuber has its energies taxed to supply food for fresh growth, which is always weaker than the first, and is productive of a diminished crop of tubers. It is not necessary at present to draw earth up the whole length of the row, but simply to mould up each plant about: two inches thick Under these conditions the frost can only injure an odd leaf that may be uncovered, which is quite a different thing from destroying a few inches of stem. PEAS are sufficiently advanced to require support. Some growers earth these up, but we have not found any advantage from pursuing the practice beyond the slight protection that the ridges of soil may give to the -young plants. This, however, cannot be the motive of the earthing-up Advocates, as they conduct the same process through the season. Those who wish to test the utility of the custom may do so by leaving a portion in the middle of each row not earthed. For short rows ,nothing is perhaps so convenient for support as sticks, but it is not wise to put the ,whole in at once, as they shade too much when every gleam of sunshine is so precious. It is much better to insert small twiggy pieces, a foot or 18 inches high; when the peas reach the top of these introduce the taller and stronger ones. Many amateurs make use of wire netting, whith perhaps in the end is the cheapest of all supports. Nets are also manufactured expressly for the purpose, and after being dipped in tar they last many years. DWARF FRENCH BEANS.—These are not appreciated so much as the scarlet runners by the majority of people. They require no supports, and in that way give very little trouble. They are also very productive;and the more that are gathered of them the more they will pro- duce. If picking is neglected, and the pods get seedy, the plants make but little progress afterwards. For ex- hibition purposes there is not a more taking bean than Canadian Wonder when nicely grown. RIDGE Cucumnens.—Unless these have been already sown, and placed in the window of the dwelling-house to forward them, the best plan is to purchase the re- quisite number of plants that have been well hardened. These, if planted on a bed consisting of some fermenting material, such as manure, bones, or a mixture of these and decomposed vegetables, will grow rapidly if covered during cold nights. Trenches made on ordinary soil and filled up with the same kind of fermenting materials is another mode of growing these that is well known to gardeners. It is important that a good southern aspect should be selected, as well as a soil that is not of a heavy, cold nature. If the natural soil is of this kind the bed system should be adopted, or ridges formed on the sur- face and covered with prepared soil. TUB FRONT GARDEN.—Pyrethrum (Golden Feather) mattires its seeds in the North, and they are so hardy that they maintain their vitality during the most severe winters, and are amongst the first to germinate in the spring. Plants from these self-sown seeds are now just large enough for handling, and may be pricked in circu- lar patches or as e continuous t dging to any beds or borders. If backed up by a few dark violas and scarlet geraniums the result is a very pretty. floral picture. At first the plants may be two or three inches distant, and when they have grown so that they meet, every alter- nate one may be pulled up. Calceolarias, if they have been properly hardened off, may be put out at once, and watered immediately after they are planted. The growth of these is very brittle, and they are subject to be broken by even moderate winds; this liability increases as the plants grow larger and the flower heads develop. In order to avoid this the plants should be planted ob- liquely, all pointing in the same direction, S 3 that a great portion of them will rest on the soil. In time they will raise themselves up, when they may have a few twiggy branches thrust in the ground neatly round, and for this purpose we know nothing better than ling or heather, such as is used for besoin making. The remnants of an old birch bosom also answers very well. Tax Wrxpow.—Arum Lily.: This may be placed out of doors, and the top must be secured to a wall or a stake driven into the ground, as from the weight of its leaves it is sure to over-balance, and most likely break the pots. Whilst in this position, watering mus4not be overlooked, or their large fleshy roots will suffer. The pots may also be plunged in the bed or border of the front garden, or the plants may be turned out of their pots and planted out in the course of two or three weeks. All plants that have been grown in the windows with the view of plant- ing out should now be turned out of doors and placed in some sheltered corner for a few days, so as to thoroughly inure them.

There are 101 propositions on the digest. The propositions affect 38 rules, there being ten relating to pay- ments to sick members, eight to the graduated scale, and seven to the charge for entrance. A large increase in the membership has taken place, and it is believed that the re- turns will show 80,000 adults, 30,000 juveniles, and be- tween 8,000 and 10,000 henorary members, or a total of 100,000,

1111 S CONVICTS BITIITON AND Cunnuinnant.—Syraptorns of mental aberration have manifested themselves in the condition of Cunningham, at St. Mary's Convict Prison, Chatham. Upon the arrival there of Burton and Cun- ningham, last week, the latter prisoner, on being taken from the covered vehicle iu which they were convoyed from the railway station, and conducted into th 3 reception room, indulged in an apparently hearty laugh, and during the period he was being diveated of his beard and hair, he manifested an air of hilarity in ill accord with his position. These ebullitions of nonchalance, succeeded as they are by periods of the utmost depression, are engaging' the attention of the prison authorities.

Mummy RIOTING. —d At Dover, on Saturday night, a quarrel took place on the North Military-road. As this road is very much used by the military, in a very sort time the number of men who were originally engaged in the quarrel considerably increased. One of the Royal Irish raised the cry, "Belle off," and a very serious fight with belts ensued. One man was very badly cut about the face and left insensible on the ground for a considerahl e time. He was at first thought to be dead, but he was attended to by the bystanders and recovered, and was ultimately re- moved to the military hospital. Another soldier in attempt- ing to escape was chased up the bill, where he was over- taken and very much knocked about. Two PERSON 3 Cur TO PIECIRS BY TRAINS.—At Aintree Station, on Saturday afternoon, two women were on the down platform, and had booked to go by the 337 train from Liverpool. They were told their train was coming in, and they crossed the line for the purpose of joining the train on the other side. Instead of it being their traio, how- ever, it proved to be the 3 30 express from Liverpool, which caught one of the women, named Evans, and literally cut her to pieces, portions of her body being taken 50 yards.— The same day, Joseph Owen and two companions were pro- Reeding along the railway to their homes at Llanfair. Be- tween Menai Bridge Station and the Tubular Bridge they crossed the line to get out of the way of the And w;ch up goods train. The 12-10 fast passenger train from Ilimor to Holyhead then Came up, and Owen was caught by the engine and killed instantaneously. He was frightfully crushed about the head, and one of his arms severed from his body. The other men narrowly escaped sharing the same fate.

&WOKING CRANE ACCIDENT.—A Shocking crane accislont occurred shortly before noon on Tuesday, at Measrs. l`trKea and Co.'s sawyard, Manchester, which resulted in the death of James Hughes, and in Lawrence Gibbose being en seriously injured that he is not expected to liva. About eleven O'clock these men, with two others, were ordered to lower a large beech tree, weighing about three tons. into the yard by means of the largo travelling crane. They had strict orders to lower the tree by hand and not by the break of the crane; but the deceased man, and the one injured, either carelessly or in forgetfulness of their instructions, left the other two to let the tree down ; the immense weight overpowered them, and the handle of ths crane, whilst whizzing round at a terrific speed, caught Hughes on the left breast and dashed him down to the ground,. 301 t. below, killing him on the spot, and at the next moment struck Gibbons a blow sufficient to send him nearly 20ft. across yard. He was precipitated upon a number of sbarp-edged pieces of timber and sustained serious injuries at the back of the head. Hughes must have been instantly killed, for he never breathed after falling to the ground. lirmansumr.—The main cause of nervousness Is indigestion, and that is caused by weakness of the stomach. LORD HOSEBEWIPS VISIT TO BERLIN. BERLIN, SUNDAY NIGHT.—The differences between the English and German Governments have entirely disap- peared, and the German Government is now on excellent terms with the present British Cabinet. Lord Rosebery spent yesterday with Count Herbert Bismarck, and to-day the Chancellor paid him a long visit in his hotel. Lord Rosebery is said to have come to solicit the arbitration of the Emperor in connectipn with the Afghan frontier dispute, and to enlist his Majesty's support to secure the execution of the Egytian financial convention. Penis, MONDAY.—The conversation, or rather conversa- tions, of Lord Rosebery with Prince Bismarck turned on three points, which were elucidated in principle at the first interview, after which Lord Rosebery sent to London a -very loeg and elaborate communication. The first of these questions related to Egypt. On this etround the Chancellor demonstrated the impossibility of England remaining there alone, and the useleseness of prolonging a situation which could end in nothing. The Somlan, said the Prince, must be left to the care of Turkey or Italy, if either would un- dertake it. Egypt and the Soudan must be entirely separa- ted, as two coentries cflite unconnected; Egypt must be protected from all danger on the side of the Soudan ; Egypt must be neutralised under a strong and popular Khe- dive, and must be made sufficiently strong to protect herself and vs defend her neutrality. Tne independence of the Suez Canal must be confided to the Goverment of the Kilt dive conjointly with those of the other nations, Eng- land being allotted a marked preponderance in the surveil- lance and the mtintenence of such independence. The second question related to Central Asia. The Prince under- took to induce Rusfia to stay where she wan long enough to give England time to fortify her Indian frontier, and to revert to the policy of defending India in India. div.p: FRENCH.

SHANGITAI, SUNDAY.—The British steamer Waverley, laden with a cargo of spelter, has been seized by the French. 30,000 POLES TO EXPELED FROM GERMANY. VIENNA, SATOEPAY.—Letters from Posen and Silesia give harrowing details of the panic and misery caused through- out the Polish population by the resolution of the Prussian Government to expel an immense number of Poles who had immigrated into these districts of old Poland, principally from Russia, dtfring recent recent years. The determina- tion of the Prussian Government to drive these unhappy people back into Russia fills them with the wildest dismay. Whole villages will be depopulated, and the wretched in- habitants escorted by Prussian troops to the frontiers,where they will be met by the Russian officials and police "charged to saperintend their re-settlement." Many in- dividuals and a certain number of families are succeeding in flying into Austrian territory, but the vast mass of the , expelled Poles, boing poor and burthened with helpless families, have no such resource. Throughout Russian Poland the terrible intelligence has cast a chill of despair as it destroys the last hope of the most miserable. Prussia is now to be as inexorable as Sibera. About 30,000 are to be expelled. Some 22,000 of these have received permits of rettlement, and vill accordingly receive a certain respite to allow them to complete their arrangements for removal. As for the 8,000 others who have received no such permits, the Government does not recognise any obligation to treat them with consideration.

„.... _ THE CONGO. Pants, MONDAY.—M. de Freycinet, Minister for Foreign Affairs, has conferred with the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Public Instruction concerning the French pos- sessioas on the Congo. It was decided that the French Chamber should be applied to without unncassary delay to ratify the Convention resulting from the Berlin Conference, and to vote the credit necessary for the effective occupation of the principal points of French Congo. FIGHTING IN NORTH BORNEO. SINGAPORE, MONDAY AFTERNOON—The people Of Kew- nag, a district ceded to the British North Borneo Company, by the Sultan of Brunei last March, have objected to the transfer, and have taken up arms to prevent its being car- ried into effect; a severe figkt occurred last week between the inhabituts and the company's forces, in which two Europeans and many natives were killed. Further fighting is anticipated. THE DELIMITATION OF CASHMERE. .

SIMLA, TUESDAY.—A British mission b being sent to Cashmere with the object of fixing the line of demarkation for the north-western fronVer of that Slate. The mission is in charge of Colonel Lockhart, who is accompanied by Major Woodhouse, Captain Barrow, and Dr Giles, and a small escort.

div.head: ANNUAL MEETINGS OF FRIENDLY
div.p: ANNUAL MEETINGS OF FRIENDLY

- SOCIETIES, &c THE MANCHESTER UNITY A.M.C., AT ABERYSTWITIL The Annnal Movable Committee of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows on Monday cotn.neuced its delioerations in the Public Hall, Terrace-road, Aberystwith. The Grand Master, Mr. Louis Wollstein, of Aaington House, Welling- ton, presided, and was supported by the Deputy Grand Master, Mr. William Grimes, of Birmingham, and the cor- responding secretary, Mr. T. Collins. About 470 delegates were present —The Grand Master, in his inaugural address, congratulated the meeting on the numerical and financial progress of the Order. Last year the society increased 14 481, or nearly 500 in excsss of 1883, and the total funds amounted to £5,804,6911 —The directors, in their report, strongly endorsed the opinion of the Chief Registrar of Friendly Societies, that valuation of the assets and liebili• ties of lodges made at such high rates as 4 and 3i per cent. interest, are deceptive and misleading. They should be content to see all the Unity valuations made at 3 per cent., if it met with the approval of the A.M.C; but whatever view might be taken, the valuer must be left untrammelled, and only be reel tired to use a higher rate of interest than 3 per cent. where there is considerable probability of its being realised. Out of 3,593 ledges,there were still 229 unregistered, and the directors recommended that districts with unregi- stered lodges should be required to take the necessary steps for becoming registered by the 31st December next; and that all districts then in default be reported to the directors, to be dealt with at their next meeting the following Febru- ary. They had taken steps to protect the interests of mem-. hers who wished to retain their position in the Order, where the lodges they belonged lied refused to register as branches. Mr. Reuben Watson, of Nottingham, the Unity valuer, had informed the directors that he had been a con- siderable loser by the last valuation, and that he considered ltd. per member would be fair remuneration for the one in progress. The directors, therefore, recommended that this amount be granted by the A.M.C. Last year the Hon. Lyulph Stanley wrote suegesting that, to save the older districts of the Unity in Lancashire and Yorkshire from collapsing, an annual levy of is. per member should be made. This, he said, would produce £23,000, which might be used as a subsidy in aid of local increased contributions in older lodges. There are, the directo-s say, other eount lee besides Lancashire and Yorkshire where the branches of the Unity are threatenea with gradual extinction, and if the society could acquieme in Mr. Stanlee's suggestion much good would doubtless result, and a vast financial improve- ment be effec•ed. If a levy et is. or 6.1. could be judici- ously imposed it should at once be resolved upon by the A.M.C., for aid to be ellec,ual must be immediate in =ay cases. The directors were of mullion that a levy of LI. per member should be made for the ireity fund required to oe provided by the Friendly Societies Act, and from the fund so formed assistance might be given to distressed lodges and districts which had for a reasonable period complied with the rules of the Order. With respect to district funeral funds, out of 365 districts which made the required re tures 323 raised funeral funds by qual levies on lodges, and only 42 had graduated on special rates of levies. GRAND UNITED ORDER OF ODDFELLOWS. The biennial conference of this Order commenced on Monday, at B.rlsenhead, under the presidency of Mr. Alfred Bailey, of Preston, Grand Master. The delegates present numbered 120 —The Grand Maser eid it was not cus- tomary at the first day's meeting for him to say anything on that occasion, but simply to ask the conference to pro- ceed to business. The first bueinese was te call over the names of the delegates appointed to represent the various districts, and he therefore requested the Grand Secretary to do this —The tellers were then appeinted, after which the Grand Secretary celled out the names of the delegates and gave to each his vas lentiels.—The remaining portion of the day's proceedings was of a formal character. FREE GARDENERS. The annual general meeting of the delegates of the National United Order of Free Gardeners was commenced at Sandbech, on Monday, the Grand Master (Bro. Roger Kemmet) presiding., Mr. James C Laird (Newcastle and Gateahead district) being in the vice-chair.—The Grand Master congratulated them on the c ,ntinued progress of the Order. The last annual return showed that they had 91 districts, 721 lodges, and 44.758 members, and that the aggregate worth of the lodge funds was £104,580, and of the district funds £12,665. b EPHERDS. The A.M.C. of the Ancient Order of Shepherds com- menced their sitting at Bristol, on Monday, the Chief Shep- herd (Mr. Duncan Kennedy, of Glasgow,) presiding. Seventy-three delegates were present. The High Sheriff of Bristol delivered a brief address of welcome. The Chief Shepherd reported that during the past year the Order had been very successful, 32 new lodges having been estab- lished, including one in British Guinea and another in Jamaica. During the last ten years £105,778 had beers dis- pensed in benefits. SONS OF TEMPERANCE (NATIONAL ORDER). The annual session of this Order was ripened in Leeds, en Monday, by the Most Worthy Patriarch (Brother Weight- man, of London), attended by 100 representatives from all parts of the kingdom. The annual report showed that the Order consists of 397 divisions, comprising over 20,000 members. Above 3,000 new members were admitted during the year. The rate of mortality in the Order only averaged 7 per 1,000, as compared with 12 to 15 per cent, in non- abstaining Orders. A scheme for the centralisation of the funds was rejected. THE AMALGAMATED SOCIETY OF ENGINEERS. A conference of delegates from branches of the Amalga- m Aed Society of Engineers commenced ito sittings in the Albert Hall, Nottingham, on Monday. Mr. Horne, of Lon- don, occupied the chair, and there were present about 240 delegates, including two from New York. Mr. Austin, of Manchester, represented the Australian branches. The ob. ject of the Conference is the revision of the rules of the society, and the sittings are expected to continue for about a month. The meeting was held with closed doors. At the end of last year the society numbered 58,681 members, distributed among 450 branches, situated in Europe, Asia, Americo', and Australasia. The total income for the year was £157,484, and the expenditure £172,811. Although the society thus spent £15,357 more than was obtained, it still had left an accumulated fund in the hands of the breeches and offices of £162,768. The A.M.C. resumed its sittings at Aberystwith on Wed- nesday. The directors' report showed that there were 593,000 members and 3,593 lodges in Great Britain attached to the Order. The report stated that proceedings had been taken to protect the interests of members in seceded lodges who,desired to remain loyal to the Manchester Unity. Ex- ception was taken to colonial and foreign deputies voting on finaseial qnestions, brat a clause in the report, deciding to make no alteration in the mode of procedure in connection with colonial representation, was finally adopted. THE CO-OPERATIVE CONGRESS. The 17th annual Ce-operative Congress has this week I been held at Oldham.—The Bishop ef Manchester preached on Sudsy the Congress sermon to the delegates. His lord- ship said he regarded tbe co-eperative movement as one of the manifold forms and developments of the progress made in the direction of emancipation from slavery. He believed the principles of the system were sound, and the movement hal deservedly met with a remarkable amount of success. It had been a great blessing to large masses of the commu- nity. Co-operators were accused of being as keen as any- one in the race for wealth, and it was also urged against them that they bad no independent auditors, and therefore their accounts were not sufficiently trustworthy. As a friend and well-wisher, he advised them to be sure that they were honestly solvent before the world, and to take care that the world knew it, and they ought also to be certain that co-operation was their true and primary object, and not merely money-making. If these two principles were not kept in view, he would prophesy that there would be no per- manency in co-operation. On Saturday a meeting of the Central Co-operaeive Board, numbering 52 members, was held to settle the terms of their report to be presented to Congress. Mr. Thor. Wilberforce (chairman of the North-Western Sec- tion of the Board) presided, and among those present were Mr. Thomas Hughes, Mr. Lloyd Jones, Mr. G. J. Holyoake, and Mr.E V. Neale (general secretary) The report ex- pressed regret that the expected improvement in the ful- ness of the Registrar's returns has been only partially realised. Includieg seven societies in Ireland there is a grand total for the United Kingdom of 1,153 societies mak- ing returns, with a total membership of 680,165, sales for the year £28,080,310, trade charges 727,875, share Capi- Jai £7,467 849, loan capital £1,524,341, net profit £2,322,203, and allowed for education £15,754. Compared with the returns, for 1882 these figures show increases in every particular except in tan capital, which ,has decreased by £70,661. The increase in number of members is 18,848, in sales £1,473,309, in Irate charges £91,881, in share capital £35.260, in net profit £209,858, and in amount granted for education £lOl5. Ihe official return of the Reeistrar only gives the figures to the and of 1883. The congress opened In the lnduitrial Societies' Hall, on Monday morning. Upwards of 500 delegates from all parts of the kingdom and some continental representatives were present. Mr. Lloyd Jones presided. In the course of his , inaugural address, he eabl the present system of distrilme live co-operation had been testest by severe, extexeive, and long-tried experiment, and had corns out of the trial trium- phantly. They ought to pay special attention to the es- tablishment of an eff 'ctive system of co-operative teaching. There was nothing more certain than that co-operative p-o- -duction was a necessity, and that the movement would never cease its experiments until it was as much a success as distributive co-opera'ion had become. In co-operative production, everything had been left so far to the chapter of accidents. Another movement which demanded their at- tention, were it only fer its magnitude, was that represented by joint-stock spinning mills, principally belonging to Old- ham and neighbourhood. There were about eighty such mills within a radius of three miles of that hall, and the capital employed could not be less than eight millions sterl- ing. They might be regarded in connection with the co- operative movement as a special growth, and required to be looked at and considered on their own merits. He con- fessed he did not accept the joint-stock system as the best on which to pursue co-operative production, but he regarded

it as a great stride in advance of the old system of indivi- dual and camartnership proprietary, and a greater advance still when shares %%ere at the price calculated te draw into such cosine the savings of working people. Joint-etock co/leaps Intved trio capacity of the working people to call them into existence and carry them on successfully. Wriat had been done in Oldham and neighbaurhood went to dis- prove and overcome the dangerous fallacy built on the as- gumption that united numbers were placed at a disadvantage :a comp. tition with individual owners of large core,. 55. There was not much that gave any one party engaged in co-operative production a right to criticise harehly the pro• ceedings of any other ; but there was much, when what bad been accomplished Was looked at, to draw them towards ' each other in mutual confidence and to held them together for the accomplishment of the great task which lay before them.—ln response to a vote of thanks, Mr. Lloyd Jones said it week' be tifty years since he was placed on the Central Beard.—The Oldham Chamber of Commerce and the Trades Council presented addresses welcoming the con- gress. An exhibition of co-operative manufactures was subse- quently opened by Alderman Buckley. In the afternoon Mr. F. Hardern read a paper on the limited liability movement, stating the working classes of the town were annually receiving from £150,000 to 2200.000. Ten million paunds were invested in local ce-operative and limited liability organisations, the greatest part belong- ing to the working olas3ee.—Mr. Greening, of London, said the pint-stock movement was a dangerous couree for co- operators to embark in, because it was not only not co- operative, but distinctly anti-co-operative.—A general dis- cussion ensued, and there seemed to be a general opinion that Mr. Greening had made out his case in opposition to the paper,--On the motion of Mr. Copeland, it was agreed that the time had arrived for new avenues of co-operative Production, and that it should be an instruction to the new board to formulate a practical scheme. On Tuesday Congress opened under the presidency of Frank Herbern (Oldham). The report of the Central Board was read, and a discussion followed. Considerable excitement has arisen consequent on the attack made on the joint-stock enterprise by the southern delegates and the reservations contained in the praise given by Messrs. Holy. oak and Lloyd Jones. Already there are statements made of a new departure in conducting joint stock mills. While the report of the Central Board was under discusion it was resolved to ask the Registrar to put in force the power which he possesses for imposing fines on co-operative so- cieties which neglect to send in returns to him. It was sub- sequently decided to request the Central Board to issue an appeal for contributions towards the Hughes Scholarship fund, which now realised £7O a year.—The Congress also end3rsed the proposal to raise a testimonial to Mr. Lloyd Jones. In supporting t'ds p:oposition, Mr. G. J. Holyouk described Mr. Jones as the most earnest, consistent, and brilliant advocate co-operation ever had. The next Congress will be held in Plymouth in Whit-week. On Wednesday Mr. W. Crooks (Blaydon) and Mr. E. 0. Greening read papers, the one on co-operative education and the other on the future of the working classes. Mr. H. Slitter and Mr. J. Maudsley attended as a deputation from the Parliamentary Committee of the Trades' Congress, and received a hearty welcome. Their presence and the paper of Mr. Greening led to further discussion about the de- sirableness of union between trade unionists and coopera- tors.

THE PRODUCTION 0 w CAST STEEL , FROM PIG IRON. At a meeting of the Glasgow Poilosophical Society held recently, Mr. W. Gorman read a paper on "The production ' of cast steel oringot iron from crude or pig iron." lee author reviewed the open-hearth system for the removal of ' impurities in crude iron. It was shown that the greatest improvement hitherto introduced consisted in adding hema- tite ore or other oxides to the bath of the molten iron, as a silicic cinder was formed all round the iron and excluded the oxygen from the atmosphere of the furnace and ren- dered necessary the addition ef oxygen in ramie form to re- ' move the carbon. Previously the neceesery supply was obtained from the silica being reduced by the iron when raised to a very high temperature. In introducing oxides to a furnace great care was necessary, he said, as a great part of the ore introduced went to form solicates. which retarded the oxidation of the carbon, pre- vented the escape of the sulphur and phosphor- ous, and dissolved the sand lining and brickwork of the furnace. The presence of silicic acid prevent d phoephor- One and sulphur from being removed. Mr. Gormaa in this connection gave a description of a furnace having two hearths, one on a higher level than the other, in which the crude iron would be melted and treated either with blasts of a'r or iron oxides for removing the silicon from the iron. When the iron was freed from silicon it was run into the , second hearth lined with iron oxides silica or slag being as , far as possible excluded. Such a furnace was designed in view of the well established facts—(l) when crude iron was surrounded by a basic cinder the impurities left the metal and entered the cinder ; (2) that the silicon could be oxi- dised from the iron by oxides, air blast, or steam in a few , minutes, leaving only a trace; (3) that the eilicic cinder floated on the top of the iron before the boil, and the iron could easily be run separately from it, so that when no salicic acid was present the refining of the iron from phosphorous and sulphur was a simple process. Having mentioned that an impression prevailed amongst ironicas- ten; that good iron or steel could not be made except from charcoal er hematite iron, Mr. Gorman stated that iron had been made at Gartsherrie Ironworks in a furnace (designed by himself in 1869 and 1874) from raw blackbend ore. In closing his paper, Mr—Gorman affirmed that, by removing the silicon by an air blast, and then refining with oxides of iron, any class of iron could be cleared of impurities to the extent required for making iron and steel. That method, he said, applied to common Scotch ores quite as much as tu hematite iron.—lrentcorkers' Journal,

NOTES BY THE WAY.

The remaining ties in the competition for the Lancashire Amateur Challenge Cap were played off on Saturday. The day, however, was not as favourabte as could be wiahed, the result being that several of tne games were left drawn. The most important matches were those between East Lancashire and Damen, and Pendleton and Oldham Borough. In the former, East Lancashire looked like being in for a sound threshing, having obtained 115, against 92 for five wickets. The Darwen men were playing a splendid game, the score being heavy and the fielding and bowling being good. In the case of Pendleton and Oldham Borough a very excit- ing finish was witnessed, the former winning by only one run. The Lancashire County Eleven opened their Season at Old Trafford, on Monday, with the Colt's match. This year there was a very large number of aspirants for County honours and the result was that 22 Colts and a captain were selected. The County team was a strong one, and included five amateurs and six professional players, while amongst the 23 were seven amateurs and 16 professioaels. The Lancashire Eleven concluded the first of the two now annual engagements with Oxford University on Saturday. The game was a splernlid one, notwithstanding that several of the leading county men were absent, and places found, among others, for Nash and Price. Crossland, contrary to expectation, was also amongst the eleven. The match of the first innings was of an even character, only nine runs separating the two "twelves" at the close of the first in- nings. Messrs. Cochrane and Bastard bowled in fine form, and four of the Lancashire team failed to score, but in the trundling department Barlow and Nash carried off the hon- ours. Lancashire were enabled to beat the University by 51 runs, and thus in some measure atone for the two de- feats last year. Lancashire concluded the second innings for 149, and when rain prevented play before luncheon Ox- ford had lost five wickets for 37. After that, however, Mr. Page, the captain, and Mr. Backland hit vigorously, and raised the total to 98, when both were dismissed—Page 47 and Bucklacd 31. The remaining batsmen only added 10 rune, and the innitip closed for 108.

div.head: CHESHIRE CIEDIBER OF AGRICULTURE.
div.p: CHESHIRE CIEDIBER OF AGRICULTURE.

A meeting of this chamber was held on Thursday at the Ciewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, to consider and discuss the pro- posal made lee Lord Egerton of 'fatten to make agricul- tural education part of the curriculum of teaching in national schools. Mr. Henry J. Tollemache, M.P., presided, and there was a fairly good attendance. Mr. Rigby (secre- tary) presented the report of the council, which referred to the action of the chamber during the past half-year in or- ganising opposition to the various bills of the railway com- pany, and also urged legislation in the matter of relief from taxation of some of the burdens pressing upon the agri- cultural community.—Ou the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr. Hollaud, the report was adopted. Mr. Rigby then read a letter from Lord Egerton, invitine discussion of his proposal to recommend the Privy Council to introduce agricultural subjects into the curriculum of board and national school teaching. Mr. Rigby also read a paper prepared by himself on this subject. He said the growing sentiment of these deeply interested in the sue- I cesaful pursuit of farming was to promote a higher or more appropriate education of the young, so as to better fit them for their duties and make them more likely to ' succeed ; and he pointed out the expression of desire ' made by the Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Association (added 'to the work they had done to improve by teaching the manufacture of cheese) as an indication that the prac- tical mind of the county was actuated by a similar wish, , and that the argument and the sentiment were both in , favour of the proposal they were considering, and he hoped I they would have no hesitation in adopting it. He suggested , - the following memorial be passed and sent to the Privy I j Council :—"That your memorialist i are largely interested I in agricultural pursuits, and are very desirous to see better technical instruction of the young in agriculture. That this might be promoted by more prominence being given to the subject, and more importance attached to its teaching I in the national and board schools of rural districts. That , elementary agriculture should form part of the course of I teaching in the higher standards in all such schools, and payment be made for results on examinations in it as in ! other subjeots. Your memorialists believe that youths I would come from such teaching to the work of the farms with more aptness to follow it intelligently, and with more advantage to themselves and the farming industry; and they therefore pray your honourable board to adopt such course as in your wisdom may best provide for this." —The Rev. J. R. Armitstead thought the subjects in their , national and day schools should be varied, and knowledge imparted on agricultural questions. He, however, recognised I the difficulty of getting their teachers and inspectors to go in for these subjects.—The Chairman said he was afraid there was ro hope of getting agricultural schools sub- sidised by the Government. —Captain Cotton said that the Dairy Farmers' Association was considering the question cf forming a dairy school, and although there were consider- able difficulties in the way, he hoped to see the object car- ried out. After further discussion an addition was made to the memorial that agricultural subjects should be introduced into night schools, and that the system should be one of payment by results; and with this addition the memorial was unanimously adopted, and ordered to be forwarded to the Privy Council. A discussion then took place upon a letter from the Central Chamber of Agriculture, requesting to know whether it was expedient to put any questions to candidates at the next election to elicit their views on agricultural question?, and, if so, on what questions.—The Chairman spoke against the proposal, thinking it might lead to the introduction of patty political queetions into their meetings, and if that were so he was afraid the inevitable resale would be that the chamb3r would be broken up, for the landlords would not continue to support it.—A telegram was read from Mr. James Tomkinson, stating what his views were in agricul- tural legislation—namely, protection to the selling tenant, compensation for disturbance, freedom from vexatious penalties, equality of other creditors with landlord. Several farmers said that the sole object of the chamber was to in- prove their position, and they maintained that as they were directly affected by legislation, the opinions of the chamber Ought to be impressed upon parliamentary candidates.—The motion that questions should be put to candidates was car- ried by a large majority, and it was left to a committee to draw up the questions and submit them to a future meet- ing.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

, iv HITSUNTIDE AT PHESCOT.—AII the shops and °the plotless of business were closed in Presoot on Whit-Monday, and the day was looked upon as a holiday. Those in the street were in holiday attire, sad many took advantage of the brightness of the weather and left town for the day ot strolled into the country. WHITSUNTIDE AT RAINHILL.—MOnday last was ob- served as a holiday in Rainhill, all places of business being closed. A number of the members of the filet and second classes in connection with the Parish Church Sunday schools availed themselves of an opportunity of an excur- sion to Wales, which, it is needless to state, was thoroughly enjoyed, notwithstanding the fact that they had to kmrney on foot to and from Clock Face Station, near Widnes. There was else a goodly numieer of visitors to the village during the day.—Rainhill Asylum Sports.—jn Whit. Tuesday afternoon -the annual sports for the instates of the Rainhill Asylum were held on the cricket field. The sports began at three o'clock, and is add tion t tt,e inmates there were present a good number of spectators, the rela- tives and friends of the inmates, who were admitted by in- vitation. The only events were hit racing for the male and female inmates, and obstacle racing, sack recinc, and wheel- barrow racing for the males. In the interval between each race the spleodid band of the institution gave selections of dance music on the green. Refresbaaenta were served out to the patients at half-past five on the green. At the close of the sports Dr. Rogers presented the prizes, which con- sisted of pipes, tobacco pouches, collirs, neckties, eatchels, em., to the winners. The proceedings terminated about seven o'clock. . _ .

_ rumor GUARDILNS —At the fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Guardians, on Thursday, the Rev. Thom as Cham- bers (Halewood) complained that a meeting of the Guar- dians had been held en Whit-Monday. He considered that as the Local Government Board observed the holiday. the Guardians ought also to be free on that day.—The Clerk (Mr. Hartley) said the duties of the Guardians were con- tinuous, but if they desired it meetings should not be convened on B ink Holidays in future.— The subject then dropped. On the motion of Mr. Newsome (Eccleston) a vote of condolence was passed to the family of the late Mr. John Fidler, guardian for Eccleston. The clerk was instructed to take the necessary steps for filling on the vacancy thus caused in Eccleston township, and also one caused in hill by by the resignation of Mr. W. A. Meadow3.—The Clerk stated that the Corporation of St. Helens had sent in a I claim for £23 133 as cost of maintenance of pauper patients in the St. Helens Infectious Diseases Hospital. He remarked that the Guardians contended that the St. Helens authorities were quite capable of looking after their own pauper pa- tients, and as a matter of fact the Corporatien hal not been asked by the Guardians to provide accommodation.—The clerk was instructed to reply that the Guardians refused te acknowledge liability.

On Monday e pleasure boat Was ca bt in a .pall off Mabeltherpe. on the Lancashire coast, tine five excursionists were drowned. It iseresid that Lord Edmond Fitzmanece will, on account of ill-healto, shortly retire from the Ural r Secretaryship for Foreign Affeirs. Tuesday night's London Gazette announces that the dAwtaßnll Blackburn, rGnloooittnna2noviedsiessede,nEaduselecoadd.:a:Cos.wafsojtrlademrnheocelets;,:Badnbgrerruaiotndali;nhbf. baronetcy of the United Kingdom has been conferred upon sWioingatn4wcaaer case David Doig, the young man wbo murdered his sweetheart at Ayr last week and afterwards Shot himself in the head, died on Monday from the Effects of the self-infiicted injuries. einewen WILL Oter.—Wm. Sheehan, who arrived nit Monday night from New Zealand, was on Tuesday remanded or at 6ork charged with murdering hie mother, brother, and npuhoelsres,.e posses- sion sister, at Castletomin 1877. The annual meeting of the Yorkshire Association of flap. list Churches Was resumed on Wednesday at liebden Bridge. The Rev. T. G. Rooky, president of the It awdon College, was elected vice-president of Vie Association. A new torpedo is about to be brought into use, the right to which the Government is seid te have acquired front its Atenrelian inventor, who is to receive a Sum VariOnlir stated at between £40,000 and £lOO,OOO as the reward of his genius. Snip DESTROYED BY Fine.—The clipper ship, Be Be Wanes, which had recently arrivei in Bangkok Harbour (Siem) from New York, with a full cargo, took fire in port on Sunday, and was tetelle thstroyed. The whole of bee !cargo was on hoard at the time, and is a total loss. Bianca/ or Peonies -A Dublin jury on Wednesday ewer- ded gloo damages to a young woman named Jana Crillye late manageress of the White Hart Hotel, Drogheda, in an action for breach of promise to marry which she brought against Sergeant Gibnei, of the Royal Irish Constabn- lary. A Dublin correspondent states that Mr Parnell, acting on the advice of a prominent member of the Irish parliamen- tary party, has determined that it is by county conventions that the candidates fer the several parliimentary divisions of each county will be selected, instead of by the division themselves separately. The Man John Taylor was brought up at Oldham Police Court, for the seventh time, on Wednesday, charged with attempting to murder, by shooting. a builder nsned Win. Whitaker. The Chief Constable described the injured man's condition as dangerous, and a further remand for eight &ye was accordingly granted. FATAL MACHINERY ACCIDENT.—On Tneedey merning, Win. Owen, 24 years cf r•ge. was killed at the mill of Messrs. R. MeClute and Sons, Heaton Norris. He was engaged in putting a strap over a pulley; when he was aught in the machinery, his body being feerfully mutilated. The de- -ceased was a grinder, but was officiating for an absent over- ' looker. RACING LOTTERIES —At London, on Saturday, three I men were sentenced to three months' imprisonment for be- ing concerned in getting up lotteries on horse races. They had been in the habit of selling tickets to clerks and others and of offering prizes varying in amount from £5OO to £lOO. The offer eves purely illusory, as the prisoners spent all the money they received. feleeseetrourea.—A qnarr. I occurred on Tuesday night between two men named Wm. Lock and John Westwood, at a public-house in East.ferry-road, Poplar. Westwood chal- lenged Lock to fight, and, encouraged by the bystanders, they did so, when a blow from Westwood struck Lock in the centre of the throat and caused immediate death. West- wood was-teken into custody. Hexane° eerie SON.—A youeg woman named Isabella Hewson Is in custody at Hull, charged on Wednesday on her own confession with the murder of her son. She ear- rendered herself at the police station, stating that she bad. hanged her little boy, and on the pence vieitinit her house they found her son suspended from tee ceiling by a piece of clothes line and quite dead. Tun VoRESEITRN COAL TRADIL—The strike of Colliers ia South and Weet-Yorkshire is gradually coming to an end. The employers of several large pits have effected a settle- ment with their hands, who have conceded the reduction originally proposed. At the Wombwell Main the colliers,. it is said, have signed contracts to resume work, and at a neighbouring colliery the miners have resumed at the reduction. hnOCHING DEATH —At Castle Pollard, Mullingar, a re- ligious Miersiea has been held, and a limeburner named Michael Farnham, and bis daughter Margaret, ahended. Ore returning home, en Moeclay, both proceeded into a limekiln to renew the fire, when the gases overcame them, and death remitted. Sublegently, a son of Farnham's went to search for his father and eider, and, going inside the limekiln, ha& a narrow escape. CHILD MoRDER.—At Nrston Police Court, en Tuesday, Annie Mitchell was charged on the coroner's warrant with the wilful murder of her child. Evidence was given to prove the finding of the body of a newly-born child on the Commo_n, neer Neaten, by a labourer, who gave information to the Cheshire police. Suspicions circumstances connec- ted with the movements of Annie Mitchell caused the police to arrest her for the murder. M. GLADSTONE AND 'THE PENSION LIST —A Conserva- tive speaker having asserted that on account of having spent a certain sum of money in a manner that was not Lonest, Mr. Gladstone had refused to produce the Pension List for 1880, the Premier's private secretary has written te Horneastle gentleman, who called attention to the matter, that the return of the Civil List Pensions for 1883-84 had been presented to Parliament ire due course A fund was not reserved for widows and orphans. Mtnerrnanns Ononeee ON A GIRL—On Tuesday af.et;:- ' noon, Titus alp'Alno,irortworker, lately of Manchester, war sentenced to six months' imprisonment for committing a murderous outrage on a girl named Harriet Green on Mon. day. Preoecutrix was sent an errand, and when efillkieg- through a field the prisoner overtook her, stabbed her, and. afterwards attempted to strangle her. The girl was found bleeding and a portion of her clothes destroyed. The prisoner denied all knowledge of the outrage. A FATAL DRINNING BOUT—William Wright was burned to death on Sunday night in a barn at Lofthouse, near Wakefield. Deceased was cne of a party of seven melt who, after drinking at various public-houses in the village of Lofthouse, adjourned about ten o'clock to a farmer's barn,. taking with them two bottles of whisky. Shortly afterwards the barn was observed in flames, and deceased wee found burnt to a cinder. The other six m2n were charged before the magnet-etre with manslaughter, and remanded. Tau VATICAN.—It may be ipnetcrheassOanggation Echnogsleisnhaßrirslemma-n (oor the Archbirhopric of Buch- abCreaesrt hot .of theichse tlp,eis,ltsae orrnneibst that Ordertolep e P , Monsignor Paoli, was well-known ' in England as the friend and associate of the celebrated Father Ignatius Spencer, the uncle of Earl Spencer. Mon- signor Paoli founded several important churches at High- gate, in Glasgow, and in Dublin. The new Archbishop, Monsignor Antonio Palma, will be consecrated at the Chapel of the Propaganda on Sunday. Tits HousING OE TUB lalsit PoOß.—The Royal Com- mission for the Housing of the Poor is under the presidency of Sir Charles Dilite, the other Commiodoners being Lord ; Brownlow, the Bishop of Bedford, the Hon. Lyulph Stanley, 1 Mr. S. Morley, Mr. Jesse Colliegs, and Mr. Gray, M.pne. At the inquiry in Dublin, on Tuesday. the examined several witnesses from the provicees. The Royal Corn mission on the housing °, the poor brought its sittings in Dublin to & cloee on Wednesday. Sir Charles Dilke and Sir Richard Cross afterwards addressed a meeting of the Ladies' Sanitary Association. StIVENNT TELEGRAMS.— The following letter from the ; Postmaster-General has appeareci in The Times :—"I shall be cbliged if you will permit me to Correct the report of my , speech on the Telegraph Bill °None point. I am reported Ito have said that the sender of a telegram need not insert in the address the name of the post office to which the message is sent. I intended to convey that the sender of a message need not give the name of the town from which he sends the message, because this information must be given in the official words of the post office, and is always written on the telegram.
