cieties have cut the Gordian knot by re-paying ! to members all moneys to their credit in the • books of the society beyond a certain sum— an honest and safe, if not a very heroic way of facing the issue. Where the rules have permitted of such a course, and circumstances have been favourable, cottages have been built for members ; and it has thus happened that men who were at one time "from hand to mouth" in their household arrangements have become owners of the houses in which they live. It may be said that, if they had taken care of their money, they might have done the same thing apart from co-operation; and this may be granted without weakening the point in favour of co-operation, that it has been the means, in the first instance, of a practice of economy being established. There are some Co-operative Societies that have been less prudent; having money lying idle, they have invested in various under- takings, with a view, of course, to profit, and in several cases, consequent upon losses, they have got themselves into difficulties. It is obvious that Managing Committees should be exceedingly careful as to what they do with surplus capital. It is a mistake to do anything which may be regarded as outside the strict sphere of co-operative enterprise, or to do anything which, at the worst, may endanger the capital of the society for which they are acting. We would emphasise this observation because of the eagerness shown at the Co-operative Congress at Oldham this I week, by an influential section of the dele- gates, to utilize surplus capital by engaging in productive co-operation. The report of the Committee specially appointed to con- sider this question was that the time is not ripe for enterprises of this kind. This may ' or may not be the case, but whatever is done I with spare capital should be done, in the first place, with the full knowledge and consent of the members of the various societies ; and, in the second place, there should be no engagement except as to capital I which can be really spared in case of loss. For instance, it would be a rash thing for a distributive society with £l,OOO of surplus , cash to invest in half-paid up shares in an I Oldham Co. operative Spinning Mill. It is possible that the mill might, as some of the mills are doing, pay a dividend of from 5 to 10 per cent ; but what if this was followed by heavy losses necessitating the I calling-up of the whole of the capital ? The ; surplus capital would be beyond reach, and! there would be a demand on the distributive society for a second £l,OOO, which might! mean its ruin. We quite agree with those who urge that, given the capital, it is a mat- ter mainly of knowledge and skill to succeed in productive as in distributive co-operation.l Oldham itself furnishes striking evidence of success. in this direction, with its So co-opera- tion mills at an outlay of eight millions ster- ling. But progress must necessarily be slow; the greater the tree the slower its growth, No I one can doubt who looks back on the hum- ble efforts of 181+ and contrasts them with what is being done to-day, that the next if not the present generation will see productive co-operation, in almost every branch, in the hands of those who have so successfully ' mastered the problem of distribution. But along with this we must have something more ; the workmen-employers must bring down blessings not only upon themselves, but upon the employed workmen, whether share- holders or not. They must all be partners in the concern in that they must ail have an in- terest in the profits, which will then be the larger in that there will be a common interest in the saving of time, and labour, and material. But better than all, co-partnership of this kind will, if anything will, reduce to a minimum the fierceness of that friction which results year by year in strikes—strikes which bring men and machinery to a stand-still, which dislocate trade, lessen the wages fund, dissipate surplus capital, fritter away hard- earned savings, mortgage the savings of the future, and bring families which should be happy to misery and starvation.

WE are glad to see that the Warrington Board of Guardians have set themselves re- solutely to the task of carrying out reforms at Padgate Industrial Schools. They were in a position, if they thought fit, to practi- cally disregard the recommendations of Mr. HENLEY, Inspector of the Local Government Board, and go their way as people who were 'beyond reproach. Some few of the Guardians seem to have been disposed •to take this course ; but the majority have listened to the voice of reason, and the result is that changes are being made which cannot but be for the better. As' will be seen from the report in another column of the meeting on Wednesday, the Sub Committee appointed to consider the complaints made by Mr. HENLEY has made certain 'recommendations, and these recommendations, after some dis- cussion; have been adopted by the Board. The first relate& to the employment of three paupers as servants at the Schools, and, in accordance with Mr. HENLEY'S suggestion, it has been determined to. transfer them to the Workhouse. , Mr. HARRISON expressed surprise that the Committee should recom- mend their transfer' seeing that it was ad- mitted that they had been useful. H.p thought it "a wise thing to utilise pauper labdur as long as the paupers were trustworthy and respectable? In this we quite agree with him—that is regarding the statement as the statement of a general principle. But the difficulty in this case is that a special prin- ciple has been set up in erecting Padgate Schools—the principle of training and educa- ting children, otherwise belonging' to the Workhouse, apart from the Workhouse aud apart from any connection with pauperism. How absurd to spend £r5,000 in building an institution to carry out this laudable object, and then ignoring the object! It would have been much cheaper, If it was required, to ex- tend the Workhouse itself in order to ac- commodate the children now stationed at Padgate. The ratepayers of the Warring- ton Union have " paid dear for their whistle ;" and having got it they are entitled to have a tune—a new tune—from it. This is why Mr. BROADBENT and others of the Guirdians propose to relegate the three paupers to the Workhouse; they are acting on principle, and they must act on principle if Padgate Schools are to be a success. With regard to the second recommendation—that which relieves Dr. SPINKS of his post as Medical Officer for the Schools; it seems to us to be a natural outcome of the complaints made by Mr. HENLEY. Apart altogether from the question of the wisdom or unwisdom of having the same medical officer for the Schools as for the Workhouse, the Com- mittee could not but regret that there was not more effectual treatment of the diseases of', the children, and at the same time feel that a change was desirable. It is suggestive of the thoughtless way in which a Board as a whole will sometimes over-ride the proposals of a Sub-Committee that, originally, it reccmmended that there should be different

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, TurnsnaY. Up to to-day the blessed silence of the recess bas been unbroken save by the gentle cooing of Sir Stafford North. cote amongst his native dales in Devonshire. Sir Stafford evidently thinks it is time he did something in the direc- tion of asserting his position. In increasing degree of late he has abrogated his functions in the House of Commons. This is partly voluntary and partly involuntary. As far as Lord Randolph Churchill is concerned, Sir Stafford North• cote has no chance. The young lordling habitually inter. pews, thrusts his chief aside, and with the tacit assent of the Conservatives, takes upon him the functions of leader. But it is noted within the last few weeks that sir S. North- cote has (voluntarily in this casc) stood aside to let Sir Michael Hicks-Beach speak for the front Opposition Bench.. This is a change which is also acceptable to the Conserva- tives. Sir Michael is not a violent declaimer in the sense that Lord Randolph Churchill is. But he can, upon occa- sion, say harsh things of gentlemen oppo.ite, and that a prima necessity in the case of a leader of the Conserva- tive party in the House of Commons. Sir Stafford Northcote is too gentle and too fair minded for the times on which he has fallen. Occasionally, goaded by the restlessness of Lord Randolph Churchill, and incited by the cheers of Mr. Onslow and Mr. Warton, he works him- self up into an appearance of wrath, and, as happened a night or two before the House rose, thunderously demands papers and hints that some criminal intent is responsible for their being withheld. Then he reaps his reward, and knows the delight of being cheered by gentlemen who sit behind. But the effort is only spasmodic. He presently glides back in his normal condition in which he treats gentlemen oppo- site, even 111r.Giadstone, as persons who, though misguided and mislead, are, after all, not hopelessly devoid of HMI ordinary sentiments of honour and uprightness which char- acterise English geetlemen. That may be all very well in Devonshire; but it does not snit the present tone of party conitct in the House of Commons, as Sir Stafford Nortbc.as bas found.

The recess, now nearly a week old, has been unusually quiet. It is clear watt has been all along suspected, that how- ever it may be with the House of Commons, the country is not just now aflame with party faction. Regarding the actions of the Government with that advantage of perspec- tive not enjoyed by London politicians, it is, on the whole, content. The Government is not blameless, as few people are upon review of five busy years of their life. But they have done their best, and on one point the country has a very strong opinion. That is, they would rather have Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues at their worst than Load Salisbury and Lord It. Churchill at their bee. The fact is the fierce faction fights got up in the House of Commons are whstly bised upon fictions. Take any stage of the negotiations with Russia in illustration. In accordance with diplomatic usage these are, up to a certain Nint, car- ried forward in secrecy. Nobody knows what the Govern- ment are doing, and, as Mr. Gladstone pointed out in the Commons the other night, it is impossible for Ministers even to contradict an erroneous statement.

The course for unscrupulous partisans is consequently clear. They have only to invent stories of " humiliation " and "surrender," accept them as if they were matters of fact, and then attack the Government upon them. Of course if the Government carried on the negotiations with Russia in the spirit imagined by Mr: Ashmead Bartlett, even Lord Randolph Churchill's denunciation of their conduct would net be too strong. The Conservatives, accepting their own flights of imagination as stern facts supply the denuncia- tion and the House of Commons is turned into a bear garcsn. The people at large, in their common-sense matter- of-fact manner, prefer to await a knowledge of fads before framing a judgment, and in the meanwhile they have a sus- foot r es oi gcni e tpyo, wceoru lads p3o, srs. iGb llya dcsotnednne,c Et a trhl picion that no body of Englishmen, drawn from any section vvieisie nut rade eHcadrt.a Gran,em sel ington, and the rest are supposed to do. The resumption of the session is looked forward to with unusual interest owing to the anxiety as to tbe next move in the relations of Cabinet Ministers. When the Honse separated last Friday things were lacking uncommonly bad. Mr. Chamberlain and Sir Charles Mike, after much protest and discussion, had finally pat up their backs and declared that they would be no party to the proposed re-enactment of coercive measures in Ireland. The approaching holi- days and the temporary cessation of Cabinet Councils pre- ' vented the crisis from coming, to an immediate head. Hay- log fired 'heir shot, Mr. Chamberlain went over to France and Sir Charles Dilke to Dublin. In the meantime the holi- days have intervened and opportunity has been afforded for seeklag a malts vivendi. Tnis I balky° will be found, and a catastrophe which would be scarcely less than fatal to Liberal prospects at the general election will be averted. The Conservatives have, naturally enough, been in a state of elation at the prospects of the general election coming on ' and finding the Liberal leaders at sixes and sevens. Mr. Chamberlain and Sit Charles Dilke would be careful to avoid the pitfall into which Mr. Forster fell, and would not consent to be made catspaws of by the eneccy. Ent they would be obliged to oppose the Government in the House of Commons on the question of renewing the Coer- cion Act, and protestations of loyalty to Mr. Gladstooe on all other matters would not avail agailast this attitude which of itself might in the peculiar circumstances of the case lead to a defeat of the Ministry. These considerations are not likely to have. been absent from the mind of the Allied Forces (Mice and Chamberlain) and expectations founded upon what took place just before the House rose are, I yen- ' ture to think, doomed to disappointment. The chairman of ,an important Southern railway observed to me a fortnight ago that he did not know what had be- corne of railway passengers. They certainly did not go by-: his line, where the reduction In traffic during the current. year is enormous. Railway managers were looking forward', to Whitsuntide as an opportunity for averaging in some small degree their lessening returns. But Whitsuntide turned out in woeful plight. Whit-Monday might have been better spelt Wet-Monday, and it was cold and windy . to boot. Not only railway traffic, but trarns and omnibasea grievously suffered, most wise people preferring to remain, at home to facing the" May weather" outside. What made the disappointment harder to bear was the fact that on Wednesday the weather changed, became distinctly warmer* and for an tour or two Londoners were privileged to see the. sun.

English &Whom will bear with interest, though not with, surprise, that their American brethren are bestirring them- selves to bring about a condition of international copyright- The Briar!) author puffers severely in consequence of the piratical tendencies of Americtn publishers. But the Atneri- can author hae reason to sympatliise with bin f•i:lCe the home-grown product, publipbed nec:ssarily at a hich price, cannot compote with the best importations which as prin- ted in fte States at a slight per centage over the mere cost of production. The practical form the movement has taken in America is original and strikinz. A number of the mast pppukr authors in the States undertake to read ausages from their own works, some of them.as yet unpublished,

Ticket were sold ate Premium, and the proceeds 'are pirte-e-d at the credit of a fu..d for carrying out the object of the authors. Several of these meetings have already been held. They take place in the afternoon, and turn out to be a great success. In connection with 0-ern I hear a funny story about Mark Twain. lie undertook to take part in one of the readings which commenced at three o'clock. On re- ceiving a copy of the programme he noticed that his name stood far Gown on the list. He said nothing, but to the astonishment of everybody appeared on the platform shortly after three o'clock in evening dress. When in due course his turn arrived, he observed in that nasal drawl which adds point to his peculiv humour : "You won't mind my coming here early in the afternoon in dinner dress, bat I • knew it would be evening before my turn Came." -1 Olivia was brought out at the Lyceum last night, and it is clear that Mr. Irving has had the good fortune again to hit upon piece that will run its hundred nights. Now-we see Oliva. on the Lyceum sbge and with the Lyceum cast it seems so 4 peculiarly fitted for the place and the people that the wonder is its production has been so long delayed. It is seven years • since Ellen Terry played the part of the Vicar of Wakefield's daughter. This was at.the Court, and though it is so far hick and so much has happened since then, I remember being struck with the mopping of eyelids and the curious sniffling that pervaded the theatre during the scene where Olivia takes leave of her little eistere. There was more

sniffling and eyelid mopping at the Lyceum last night in proportion as it is a larger theatre than the Court. Ellen Terry was as simply natural as ever, and in Its \lca Mr, Irving has found a character in which he_will be seen wi:h . _
infinitely more Weasure than as Hamlet: Romeo, or men Shylock.
Whilst the Lyceum has entered ripen a noir lease of pros- perous life, things are not looking so well for other theatres. The Inventories is exercising in this airection the baneful . .

influence bewailed in the ;me of the Healtheries and Fisheries. I hear of one well-known theatre manager, but yesterday the autocrat of several houses, who hae lost his all, a sum which at one time must have been considers ,le. * It is au older story how F. B. Chatterton, whose name was long connected with Drury Lane, wanders ghost-like round the scene of former triumphs. They got up a baneflt for him the other day, and now be has set up as professor of elocution, and will, if you please, train you for the stage. Sic transit qloria ntundi. A great deal too much has been made of the wilful , destruction of pictures in the Academy. The scratching is rery minute. It would be quite possible to see these pic- tures and not notice the defects, The mystery is not that the mischief should have been done, but that it should have been so little. If the malicious person bad made for the faces instead of the feet and the drapery the damage ralght have been serious. Certainly the occurrence and the cap!. ' tal that has been made out of it by the daily papers has made these special canvases well talked of and Ist II stared at. It is amusing to see hi w the crowd collect rourd the scratches. A few years ago a Turner was found stabbed right through the canvas, and the malefactor was arrested. He proved to be a poor copyist, who had made repeated failure to reproduce the great master's work, and inch spair and rage bad driven his palette knife through the picture. There is no such explanation for the Burlington House mystery.

The Board, after a painful experi- ence, has now come to the conclusion that this is the wisest thing to do, and we do not doubt that the public will approve of theif decision. It is somewhat hard on Dr. SPINKS that he should be deprived, as one member put it, of a portion of his ,emoluments ; but it should be remembered that it was very hard upon the children to let them suffer from the itch so long—a disease which, to quote the words of the Inspector, "could be eradicated at once." Mr. BROADBENT did well to point out that a good deal had been said about showing " consideration to the medical officer and other individuals, but not one had said a word about the considera- tion they should pay the children." That, however, is nowbeing done ; the Guardians, with the facts before them, have been brought to a sense of their duty, and, if they continue in the new and better way, there can be no question that a great improvement will be effected in Padgate Schools.

" Thoughts upon Demoeracy " and "The Duties of Man " are the titles of two essays by the late JOSEPH MAZZINI, which have been issued in a cheap form with a view to their getting into the hands of the working classes of this country. They are accom- panied by a lengthy and carefully written memoir by the original translator, Mrs. E. A. VENTURI, and altogether they are a wonderful sixpenny-worth. We can imagine the eagerness with which a work of this kind would have been purchased in the old Chartist days, when the people of this country, as well as of Italy, were struggling to be free. An extract now and again was as much as could be got of MAZZINIIS works —such a reproduction as the one before us being at that time out of the question. The editor in making this venture says : 1." No pecuniary profit is expected or desired , from the publication ; but it is hoped that this eloquent memorial of a noble , patriot and a good man may awaken a , true patriotic enthusiasm in the hearts /of many young English readers ; and, further, that the principles set forth by MAZ- ZINI in his essays may help to the forma- 1 tion of wise and just political opinions." MAzziNt was indeed a noble patriot, and no one can rise from the perusal of his essays, or the memoir, without feeling the moral stimu- lus of his lofty thought and exalted virtue. His aim was the regeneration of Italy, and he continued to toil to accomplish it when others despaired; but at the same time he was actua- ted by a pure love for humanity the world over, He believed in a " holy alliance," not of kings, but of peoples; and there is great need even today to study and act up to his teachings. He was a man wonderfully en- dowed, and with such gifts as he possessed he could with ease have attained eminence in any profession; but he chose rather the hard and thorny path in devoting not only his talents but his life to the people. Such souls come among men rarely, and they should be revered when they do come. The rising generation knows little of MAzz.m, and would do well to know more. The student of politics, whether old or young, will find much to strengthen, sustain, and elevate in "Thoughts on Democracy and "The Duties of Man ;" the work is one which we can confidently and earnestly re- commend to our readers.

The poor law returns for Run- corn Union showed that during tha half year ended Lady Day, 1885, the amount expended in maintenance £Bl4, out relief £1,728, tital £2,342.—Mr. Norman said this was a decrease upon previous periods.— The Clerk said the difference was in the out-door relief. IMPORTANT TO ALKALI DIANCFACTI7RERS.—We under- stand that an agreement has just been concluded among British makers of alkali which will very seriously affect the soda trade. For some time that trade has been carried on in the face of increasing competition between the makers who work by the old (or Leblanc) process of manufacture, and those who have adopted the ammonia process. Pi ice have fallen very low in consequence, soda crystals being now £2 Os on the Tyne, which is very much below the rate of a year ago. It has now been arranged that the makers of soda by the older process shall largely reduce their pro- duction of soda or ash crystol soda, or both. This arrange- ment will come into force in the beginning,.of July, and is expects,' to cause an increase in the price of soda products I generally. The agreement is on the lines of the arrange- ment made some time ago by the producers of bleach'ng, powder, which has driven up the price of that article over 50 per cent, during less than two years. The latter arrangement, however, is an international one, while that just arrived at by the makers of alkali is confined, so far, it is understood, to the producers of Great Britain.— Times.

Wa regret to have to record that there ' is a good deal of feeling in Warring on as to the date of Walking Day. The third Friday in June seems to have been accepted, until ,it was unfortunately announced by our contemporary that the MAYOR had fixed the !date for Newton Race Friday—the Friday previous. It transpires that this announce- ment was premature so far as the MAvoa was concerned ; and it was followed, last Saturday, by an express statement on be- half of his Worship that Walking Day would be on the. 191 h. This date, while meeting the wishes of Sunday School authorities, and those who have made arrangements with railway companies for trips, has proved unsatisfactory to those who prefer Newton Race Friday. An out-door meeting, which was well attended, was therefore held on Thursday evening ; and a resolution was carried, though with a narrow majority, in favour of having Walking Day in Race Week. Following upon this gathering, the MAYOR was besieged by - rival deputations, and the fullest opportunity has therefore been given him to consider the pros and cons of the case. Having regard to the fact that arrangements have been made which could not be altered without incurring great inconvenience, his Worship yesterday issued a placard stating that he adhered to the third Friday in June—that is the r9th— as Walking Day. This will be disagreeable. doubtless to those who want the holiday in Race Week as heretofore ; but, as it is under- stood that next year the date will be fixed by a thoroughly representative body, it is hoped that the best will be made of what has proved a difficult situation by loyally accepting the Mayor's decision.

PRESENTATION TO A WIDNF.9 MANAGER.—Mr. J. H. Lewis, manage cf Messrs. James Muspratt and Sons' chem- ical works, Widnes, V(l9 on Friday last week the recipient of a handso ne tetnimony a the respect acid esteem of the foremen and woikmen under his earl,. By his genial cour- tesy nil his uprig t dealings Mr. Lewis has won the re•pect• ful admiration of the men, who determined to show their feelings in an appropriate way on the first opportunity. The completion of Mr. Lewis's tenth year as manager provided the desirrd occision, and in the presence of the assembled men on Friday be was presmled with a beautlful bronze timepiece, chastely decorated in gold and silver. Mr. James L. Muspratt was present, and in a brief speech eulogised the personal qualities and abilities of Mr. Lewis. The ab- sence of Mr. E. K. and Mr. L. K. Maspratt was apologised for, business engagements preventing their attendance. Mr. F. Bite, a foreman, made the presentation on behalf of the men, expressing the hope that the good feeling which pre- vailed between misters and men would continue, and that Mr. Lewis, whose sterling abilities and goodness of heart had endeared him to them, would live long to fill his pre- sent position.—Mr. Lewis feelingly responded. He had always tried to do his best to men and masters, and had endeavoured In looking after the interests of one not to neg- lect the interests of the other.—Three ringing cheers were then given for Mr. Lewis and his son at the call of Mr, J. L. Muspratt, and the ceremony concluded.

POACHING AT LOWER WALTOIC—At Daresbury 'Petty Sessions, on Monday, two rather rough-look- ing men named James Shaw and Michael Mulkearn were charged, with trespassing in pursuit , of game on land at Lower Walton, in the occupa- tion of John Fryer, on the 30th April. On that day I John Smith, gamekeeper to Sir Gilbert Greenall, ,' saw prisoners on the ground in question with a stag hound. Mulkearn was drunk, but Shaw did not appear to be so. Prisoners' defence was that, being drunk, they missed the footpath and wandered in the field. They were each fined 20s and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. . A POLLUTED WELL AT WALTON SUPERIOE.—On Tuesday, at Daresbury Petty Sessions, Mr. John White, Latchford, Warrington, was summoned at the instance of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Au- thority, to show cause why a well at Walton Supe- rior, in the occupation of Alfred Broady, the water of which it is alleged is polluted, should not be closed in accordance with the Public Health Act.— Mr. White said that a notice was served in October last, that the water was unfit for drinking purposes, and notice WM given to Mr. Broady, the tenant, , that he was not to use it for domestic purposes. I He (the tenant) was instructed to get water from • another well. Mr. Broady gave instructions to his servants not to use the wate; and to the best of his belief they had not done so. It was intended that the well should be cleaned forthwith. Mr. Broady was in a position to state that the water would not be used. There was reason to believe that if the well was cleaned the water would be permanently good. The water should be analysed, and if not satisfactory the well should be done away with.— Mr. Farrington, inspector of nuisances for the prose- cuting Authority, said that the question had arisen from a report of the medical officer, saying that there had been a case of typhoid fever at the pre- mises in question. A servant of Mr. Broady had had typhoid fever, and she might have drunk of the water contrary to Mr. Broady's knowledge.— Dr. Adams, the medical officer of health, spoke to a serious case of fever having arisen. There were . .

several ways of getting typ— hoid fever, but the general cause was bad drinking water. In his opinion, from the analysis taken, the water was such as to cause typhoid fever. The fever was sometimes due to bad drainage.—The Bench made an order for the well to be closed to the .satisfaction

WHITSUNTIDE AT LYMM. OR Whit-Monday Lymm had an animated appearance owing to the large number of persons who visited the village from the surrounding districts. The shops were closed throughout the day, which was observed as a general holiday.. During the week, especially on Thursday, large numbers of pleasure-seekers en- tered the town. Over 1,000 arrived by train on Thursday, and some 400 alighted from trains on Friday. On the whole the weather has been favourable. SINGULAR BANKRUPTCY CASE AT WARRINGTON. —At Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour judge Ffoulkes, Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, made an application for an order of adjudication in bankruptcy in the matter of Richard Spann, wheel- wright, Friars' Green. It was, he said, an ez parte application which he made under sub-section 11 of section 18 of the Bankruptcy Act, 1883. Affidavits had been filed to prove that the consent of the Court to a composition was obtained by fraud, and he submitted that if fraud had been used to obtain a composition it should be set asiie by his Honour, and Spann should be adjudicated a bankrupt. He made his application on behalf of Mr. Garland, ironmonger, Warrington, one of the creditors, and the evidence which he ' was prepared to bring forward was the affidavit of a •man named Chapman, who vas in the employ of Spann as foreman wheelwright for about four years. The affidavit set forth that Chap- man had, at the request of Spann, removed a quan- tity of goods from the premises to various places, and that a number of books and papers had been destroyed.--His Honour remarked that what he had before him was that the creditors had ,approved a composition of 4s. in the and there was only one dissentient, who was now bringing the matter for- ward. He did not think it would be right to set aside that composition.—Mr. Davies thought his Honour would admit that the approval of the court had been obtained by frau.d.—His Honour pointed out that Chapman, whose affidavit had been read, and another person mentioned in the case, could not be independent witnesses, and if there had been a fraud they were parties to it.--Ultimately the Judge decided to take the application next Monday.

TREAT TO SCHOLARS AT RIIROSEN.—About 20 scholars of the Presbyterian Sunday school were on Tuesday treated to a trip to Hale through the kindness of Mr. Richard Evans. The children were driven from Widnes in waggon- ettes, a meat enjoyable afternoon being spent in the plea- sant village. Tea was provided. ACCIDENT TO A lirwooax TRADESMAN.—Mr. S. Coventry, tailor and outfitter. Church-street, Runcorn, met with an accident at Rhyl. In company with Mr. J. A. Smith, he was riding a tricycle down a kill in the town when he lost control over his machine. Mr. Smith endeavoured to get his tricycle out of the way but failed, and the two machines collided. Mr. Coventry was thrown heavily to the ground, and was partially insensible for some time, and it was feared that he was internally injured. Happily these fears proved groundless although his arm was severely bruised, and he was severely shaken. TOLtneritnia Pion SHOOTING COMPETITION AT WIDNES. —ln Connection with the Widnes companies of the 21st L.R.V. a challenge cup competition has just been Institu- ted The cup, which is called the " Wareing Challenge Cup," is worth £5, and has been given by Capt. Wareing. In addition there are ten money prizes. The competition has to be decided in three contests, the distances being 200 and 500 yards, and seven shots at each distance. The first contest took place on Saturday. Below are the ten highest scores :—Private J. Foster 62, Sergeant Junor 61, Private Campbell 57, Sergeant Davis 58, Sergeant Dwerrybouse 56, Private Roberts 50, Sergeant Winfield 46, Private CM- burn 43, Private Mutch 42, Private Murphy 39. There is also a second series of ten money prizes to be competed for , by members who shoot in the first series but fail to take a ' prize. Sergeant &owe is the hon. secretary for the com- petition. The minutes of this committee stated that the Clerk re- ported that Mr. Bancroft was still of opinion that. there was sufficient water on the present site to supply Frodsbam by gravitation. It was resolved unanimously, on the motion of Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton, seconded by Mr. Thomas Hadfield, that Mr. Bancroft lie instructed to prepare a com- plete plan and estimates for the Local Government B ard for the supply of Frodsham with water by gravitation from the land of the trustees of the late Major Ilitchen, and that there be shown in the plans how the supply should be Im- plemented from the springs at Five Crosses, if found neces- sary in the future. The estimates were also to inclndd the costs incurred in connection with the negotiations with owners below Mr. Wright's springs at Five Crosses, and all law charges and costs in testing for water at Newtown, and complete the whole works necessary for sufficiency of water supply for the town of Frothham. The appointment by Mr. Bancroft of Mr. Samuel Davies as clerk of works over the Frodsham (Iverton) sewerage. The minutes were passed. A letter was now read from Mr. Bancroft reporting that Mr. Dale bad carried out his contract for the Frodshans Newtown sewerage in a satisfactory manner.

KEEPING AT year LENGTH—" Your beau stems very bashful," said a Drayton avenue mamma to her daughter." "Bashful !" echoed the daughter, "bashful's no name for it." "Why don't you encourage him a little mere? Some men have to be taught how to do their courting. He's a good catch." 'Encourage him !" said the daughter, "he cannot take the molt palpable hint. Why, only last night, when I sat all alone on the sofa, and he perched up in a chair as far away as be could get, I asked him if he didn't think it strange that a man's arm aid a woman's waist veened always to be the same length, and what do you think he did?" "Why, just what any sensible man would have done—tried it." "He asked me if I could find a piece of string so we could measme and see if it was so. Ain't he horrid ?" Two BROTHERS OF THE BUSH AND 1101 V THEY BRUSHED EACH OTHER.—A certain artist named Reinagle, a contem- porary of furner, was notorious for the wildest eccentricity of manner and character. In the year 1846, on the occasion of one of the usual luncheons at the Royal Academy given during varnishing days, when only the members and asso- ciates were present, some time after thea.neal had com- menced, Reinagle burst suddenly into the room. In answer to inquiries as to his reason for being late, he explained that he had hit at last upon an excellent plan for making money. He was going to start a railway to convey passengers up and down Cheapside, and he should make his fortune in a month or two. "And then I shall give you all commissions," he went on to say in a highly-excited manner; "and you shall paint me something toe, Turner, if only you'll be good enough to tell me which way up to hang the picture when you send it home." "My dear fellow," answered Turner, '•I don't care a rap which way you hang it, if only you pay use for it."

MANCHESTER RACES. These races have been held during the past week. ! Thursday—the Cup Day—is naturally considered the principal one of the meeting, and it was not to be ! wondered at that such an immense; concourse of spec- .lators assembled to witness the day's sport, which, however, with the exception of the Cup, was again of a very tame description. The weather was not so bright as on the two previous days, but, though rain , threatened all the afternoon, the programme was gone through before any fell. Anything but a promising ' start was made when only three went to the post for the opening event, the Thursd ty telling Stakes, in rl which backers made a good beginning by laying odds ; of 5 to 4 on the Little Nell fiily, who ran very well for ! some distance in the Wednesday Selling Twceyear• old Stakes. The favourite had.no difficulty in dispos- ing of her two opponents and won easily, after which ! she was bought in for 170 guineas. For the Public ! sale Stakes only four turned out, and no sooner were the runners known tivn a warm favourite was found in Mr. T. Jennings'e Beaulieu. who has pre. vionily shown more than average merit, for he ran a good horse when finishing third to Bard and Athel- stan in the Molyneux Stakes at Liverpool, whilst he has since run away with the Two-year-old Stakes at the Second Spring Meeting at Newmarket. The olds laid on him were never in doubt, as he won with plenty in hand by a length. Another quartette con- tested the Duchy Welter Handicap, and though 7 to 4 was laid on that old slave Lyric, he was unable to gallop when Archer asked him, and pulled up very ler weary, the winner turning up in Mr. W. l'Anson s Hambledun. Preparations were now made for the principal item in the week's programme, and the partisans of each of the fifteen, competitors were eager , to catch a passing glance at their particular fancies las they circled round the saddling paddock before Ihaving the finishing touches put to their toilet. The '• • • favourite, Borneo, was voted on all hands as being in splendid condition, and showing a better trained ap- pearance than he has previously exhibited, while Grim Tartar, though slightly on the big ride and ! evidently wanting more work, found many friends. Indeed, every one of the competitors had both ad- mirers and detractors which at once found vent in the betting. Borneo held his own persistently to the end, finishing at 5 to 2, whilst the admirers of Grim Tartar were content to accept 5 to 1 about his chance. Of the others Pizarro had most friends, and 100 to 15 was freely taken, and at a point longer odds Eurasian fairly held his own. The race requires very little comment, for, though Sandiway jumped of in front of Borneo, as soon as they had settled down the favourite headed the Duke of Westminster's representative, and making the re- mainder of the running won easily by a length from Xema, who, it is only fair to say, was slightly inter- fered with on making the turn into the straight, and Cromo-a.boo. another 33 to I chance, was third. The victory was a very popular one, and the horse and rider were loudly cheered as they were led to the door of the weighing-room. The two remaining events on the card produced very little interest, the Lambton Plate only bringing out two runners. The backers of Blitz, however, at 2 to I on were destined to go down, as Prince Rudolph secured the verdict by a head. Strathblane was made favourite for the concluding event, the Stamford Welter Handicap, and after waiting on his field until reaching the half distance he then drew away and won easily by half a lengt h.

.„. COLD IN MICIIIGAN.—" Cold in MiclaigAn ! Well. some, but cold weather is good for lots of purposes. The curiousest thing cold weather's good for, is stocking fish ponds." "Stocking fish ponds !". That's so. Down to Saginaw Bay, the fishermen catch pickerel and sturgeon. Quick as they pulls 'em out they hangs 'em to freeze In about an hour's exposure to the atmosphere them fish is froze es hard as China. Sometimes they get too brittle and break all in pieces. They carries these fishes off to their inland homes, an' when spring comes they thaw 'ern out gradual. When they begin ter show signs of life—" "Signs of life !" "Yes. Two hours of lukewarm water'll make 'em lively as crickets; than they restores them to their native eta:cent, and all goes lovely. May I never take another chaw of whisky of I ain't seen it done scores o' times." A dead silence settled over the crowd, like the hush of a tired buzz. saw.

ACCIDENT AT COLLIN'S GREEN. A lad named Haworth, resid ng near the Railway Station, Collin's Green, mA with a serious accident on Monday. He WAS employed at the Collin's Green Colliery, and was following his customary occupation on the pit bank, when a large sheet of iron fell on one of his legs, which was fractured. The suff -ring lad was afterwards removed to the St. Helens Cottage Hospital. THE SALVATION ARMY AT EARLESTOWN.—A number of the members of the Warrington corps of the Salvatice Army visited Earlestown on Whit-Monday, and their move- ments created considerable interest in the town. They were led by the Salvation Army brass band, and as they marched through the principal streets large numbers of persons assembled to witness their " demonstration." During the day special services were conducted on the Market-place, and these were largely attended. THE LOWTON ROSE QUEEN.— 0 u Saturday next the ceremony of crowning the ROS 9 Queea is to be observed at Low ton, and will take place in a field in the occupation of Mr. Sweetluve, Church-lane. Complete arrangements have been made. There will be a procession to start at two o'clock, the Queen will be crowned at four o'clock, and dancing, plaiting of the Rose Pole, and various gatnes will follow Bands will play until dusk, and if the weather prove favourable a merry day may be expected. WurT-Morenalt.—Whit-Monday was obecrved at Earlestuwn by the shopkeepers closing their places of busi- ness for the day. There was an absence of trips, picnics, or amusements of any kind, and the exodus by train was comparatively small. This, in a great measure, is due to the fact that the large works in the district do not recognize Whitsuntide as a holiday, race week being observed instead. At Newton, however, there was a fair gathering of holiday makers, from the outlying towns, the principal attraction being the lake, which during the day presented an animated appearance. Shortly before noon on Monday about 100 carters from Liverpool, connecttd with a Gospel and Tem- perance Mission to carters, arrived at Newton en their annual picnic. They spent the afternoon at the lake and its vicinity, and partook of an excellent tea supplied by the Misses Birehead, of Newton, in the Town Hall.

GOOD TEILPL ARS. —The usual session of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Goad Templars Was held in the Lodge Room, IL idge-stieet, Earlestown, on Monday evening, Bro. George Clarke presicUng. After the usual routine business, several special matters were brought up. It was also unanimously resolved that copies of the following resolu- tion be forwarded to the Right Hon. W...E. Gladstone, M.P., and to the Right Hon. Hugh Childers, M.P., Chan- cellor of the Exchequer, viz :—"That this Lodge, im ses- sion assembled, would strongly protest azainst yielding to the opposition shown to the Budget by brewers and spirit dealers, whose traffic in intoxicants produces so much crime, pauperism, and insanity as would burden sober people with evils far outweighing the taxation levied upon the manufacture and sale of strong drinks. We therefore trust that a firm resistance will be offered to the attempt to evade this m-derate a4dition proposed to be levied upon them, and which very many dealers are already anticipating by raising their retail prices." An interesting session closed in the usual way at 9-45. . _

LIBERAL Manmet AT Astivon.--00 Thursday evening, an enthusiastic meeting in connection with the —Liberal Association of the Newton Parliamentary Division Was held at Ashton. Mr. C. Pilkington, J.P., presided. After an interesting lecture by the Rey. D, S. Prosser, of Walkden, on "The Present Government—A Vindica- tion." the following resolutions were unanimously passed: ", That this meeting expresses its unabated _confidence in her Majesty's present Government and approves of its policy as regards both home and foreign affairs," and "Trutt this meeting considers Colonel McCorquedale, J.P., a fit and proper person to represent this division in the next Parliament, and pledges itself to use all legitimate means to secure his retttrn." It was also resolved that copies of the resolutions be sent to the Prime Minister and Colonel McCorquodale, J.P. SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—On Whit.Senday, the anniversary sermons in connection with the Congregational Church were preached by the Rev. J. W. Walker, HA., of Huyton, and in the afternoon Ur. Walker gave an address to the teachers and scholars. The attendance at the three services was very good, particularly in the evening, at which litany persons of various denominations were present. The two sermons and the address were very appropriate for the occasion, and were heard with much interest and pleasure. At the morning and evening services the church choir sang an anthem in good taste. As the collections of previous years have not been sufficient to defray current ex- penses, it was resolved to raise a larger amount. The Sunday school scholars, by means of collecting cards, ob- tained £I2 Is 6d, and this ameent added to the eollections reached the handsome.sum of £43 5s 41, a larger collection than any previous year. PRIMITIVE METIToDIST TABERNACLE, LODOE L._ The usual weekly temperance meeting under the auspices of the above was held on Saturday evening, the room being nicely filled. Mr. Byrom, of Bryn, presided, and gave an encouraging address, after which Miss Guttridge sang a song, and was followed by Miss B. Whittle, who recited "Take Warning "very nicely. An address was then given by Mrs. Picton, and Mr. Peter Balleck sang "0 seek that beautiful stream." Mr. J. Partlngton, of Bryn, next gave an interesting and eff2ctive address on the various aspects of the temperance question. An instructive reading was next given by Mr. George Clarke, of Earlestown, and Mr. John Thompson, of Earlestown, followed with a song "The children and the drink." Mr. George E. Warburton re- cited " Nelly's Christmas box" in a most effective style, and on being recalled gave "Somebody's mother." A solo, "Out of the mine," was sung by Miss E. Clarke, of Reties- town, in a very pleasing manner ' • and Mr. Dands rendered a song, "0 the parting," satiefactorily. " The Factory Chimney" was recited by Mr. George E. Warburton, of Earlestown, in his usual good style, and a melody, " Touch I not the cup." by Miss M. E. Clarke, Miss E. Clarke, Mr. ' John Clarke, and Mr. George Clarke, brought the pro-. gramme to a close. A vote ef thanks to the chairman and en- tertaiders was heartily accorded.

EARLESTOWS' FOOTBALL CLUB.—This club (winners of the Liverpool and Dietriet Challenge Cup) concluded its season's fixtures on Saturday lest. The late season has been a remarkable one in several respects. Out of the first eight matches Earlestown won four and lost four, and scored 26 goals, while their opponents also scored exactly 26 goals. Out of the next 17 m Itches Eeriest awn was only defeated once (Crewe Alexandra. at Crewe), and they scored 62 goals, while they lost only 16. After defeating Everton in the final tie for the Liverpool and District Challenge Cup, Ear- lestown only won one out of the next nine genus, and se-iced only 11 goals, while the:r opponents ran up a total of .35 goals. The first and last matches of the season were against II iydock Temperance, who sustained a defeat on each occasion. On the whole the club has had a most suc- cessful season, and one of which its supporters should feel proud. The possession of the Liverpool and District Cballenge Cup and the Wellington Challenge Cup is a tribute te their prowess. In all 39 matches were played, of which 23 were victories, 12 defeats, and 4 games were drawn, Earlestown scoring 120 goals to 81 by their oppo- nents. The victories have been over Oswestry (holders of the Welsh Challenge Cup), at Oswestry, 3 goals to 2; Ever- ton, at Liverpool, 1 to 0 • Bootle (twice), at Bootle, 2 to 0, and at Earlestown, 3to ; Liverpool and District, at Ear- lestown, 4te 2 ; Ribchester, at Earlesto an, 10 to 2 ; Pres- ton Parish Church, at Preston, 5 to 1; Haydoce Temper- ance (twice), 2 to 1 at Haydock, and 2 to 0 at Earlestown ; Liverpool Stanley, at Earlestown, 2 to 0•, Birkenhead, Argyle, at Birkenhead, 6 to 1; Birkenhead Club, at Earles- town, 6to 0 ; Earlestown Wanderers, 8 to 2 ; C. LANCASHIRE litleBARS 110E911 COMPETITION. The annual inspection of the troopers' horses in connection with the Lancashire Hussars who last week had their annual week's training at Southport, took place on Friday. The prizes were awarded as fellows :—A Troop ( Ashton-in-Makerrield) : let prize, Corporal Pendlebury ; 2nd, Private Leach; 3rd, Private Hasleden. B Trooo (St. Helens, Wigan, and neigh- bourhood): Ist, Corporal Fairhurst ; 2nd, Private Alker ; 3rd, Private Green. C Troop (Newton and Liverpool) : let, Private J. Ellarn ; 2nd, Private W. Bond ' • 3rd, Corporal W. Gilbert. D Troop (Ormskirk and Lathom) : Ist, Pri- vats Stringfellow ; 2nd, Private Rotheram ; 3rd, Corporal Spencer. The prizes for the best young horses in D Troop were awarded as follows :—lst, Pfivate Twist ' • 2nd, Pri- vate Aspinwall. The regimental prize was won by Corporal Fairhurst of B Troop. The judges were Captain A. R Gladetone, Captain Hepworth, and Veterinary-Surgeon Dixon. '1 he annual inspection of the regiment took place on Saturday afternoon, on the shore opposite the Palace Hotel, Birkdale, the reviewing officer being Lord R. D. Kerr. Amongst the ladies and gentlemen present were Cap- tain Earle's party, Mr., Mrs., and the Misses Pilkington and party, Roby Hall ; Mrs. Herbert Pilkington, Huyton ; Mrs. Earle, Roby. There were on parade about 250 of all ranks, including the following officers : Colonel the Right Hon. the Earl of Lathom (the newly appointed commanding officer), Major F. W. Eerie, Adjutant Moreland (captain sth Lancers), Captain the Hon. W. C. Gerard, Captain A. R. Gladstone, Captain E. R. G. Hopwood, Lieut. H. J. Walmesley, Lieut. J. C. Edwards-Moss, Lieut. ff. F. de Trafford, Lieut. W. L. Pilkington, Lieut. J. H. Stock, Lieut. T. Earle, Surgeon-Major Beaman, Regimental Sergeant- Major Easthaan, Qaertermwer-Sergeant Caldwell, and Veterinary-Surgeon Dixon. The inspecting officer was re- ceived with the customary general salute, after which the , regiment was put through a variety of cavalry movements, the soldierly bearing and smartness of the men being much admired by the spectators. At the conclusion of the inspec- tion, Lord R. D. Kerr congratulated them on the efficient manner in which the different movements had been execu- ted. The men were then marched back to their respective billets. The annual church parade took place on Sunday morning, when those belonging to the Church of England attended Divine service at Holy Trinity Church, while those of the Catholic body went to St. Matie's Church in Be:thank-road. The band preceded the regiment both to and from the church.

The Rev. Thomas Elias Lyon, LL.B., of Leeds, preached the Sunday school anniversary sermons in connection with this place of worship on Sunday. In the afternoon,an in- teresting service of song was rendered by the school children and choir. The collections realised' over £3B. DEATH MON APOPLYXY.-0E Tuesday afternoon an elderly man named Ryan, residing in Lyon-street, was fol. lowing his employment at Messrs. Pilkington Bros; Crown Glass Works, when he was seized with apoplexy. Dr. Knowles, the company's surgeon, was immediately in at- tendance, but pronounced the case hopeless. Ryan was taken home on the ambulance, but died during the night. AccznaNT To A Commx.—About nine o'clock on Wednesday night a collier named Stanley, who lives at Eccleston-lane-ends, was at work in the Sutton Heath Col- liery, when a large atone fell from the roof and alighted on the lower portion of his leg and foot. He was at once taken home, and Dr. Stonhatn sent for from St. Helena, The in- juries were of a serious nature, and one toe had to be am- putated.

Walsh, acting on information received, visited the lodging-house where the accused resided. On searching the bed he found between it and the mattress a watch and chain of which prisoner could give no account. She was remanded until Friday. I Tan 21st L.R.V. (ST. HELENS) BAND.—On Wednes- day, by order. of Lieutenant-Colonel W. W. Pilkingtonr commanding the 21st L.R.V., the band of the regiment ' again proceeded to the front of the St. Helens Town Hall, 1 and played a selection of popular pieces. A large number of people assembled. It is hoped that this Wednesday even- ing performance, which only remains to be known to be thoroughly appreciated by the public generally, will be con- tinned during the summer month.. SWINE Fzvan —At a special meeting of the Health Committee of the St. Helena Corporation, on Wednesday. 1 the Town Clerk submitted an order of the Privy Council declaring the borough of St. Helene to be an infected area. 1 In addition to the inspectors tinder the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act (Superintendent Johnston, Inspectors Heigh- ley, and Whitaker, and Mr. Dixon, yeterinery surgeon), the following were appointed to grant licenses for the move- ment of swine in, into, and out of the borough :—Police- sergeants Pollitt, Gilligan, Canister, Ross Kilsbaw, and Police-constable Caunce. There are now 18 cases of disease in the borough. BURNED TO Duni Thomas Dunfey, eleven months old, eon of Michael Dnafey, a labourer living in Victoria-street, died about twelve o'clock on Tuesday at noon from injuries received on the 18th inst. On the fore- noon of the latter date Mrs Dunfey left home for a few minutes, leaving two children, aged five and three years re- spectively, with the deceased, in the house. While she was away, a neighbonr heard the obilAren screaming, and it was found that the deceased' clothing was on fire. The flames were extinguished at once, and Dr. Twyford's assistant at- tended to the injuries. The child, who was badly burned about the lower parts of the body, died as stated. Sr. lIRLENS CYCLISTS' Cram.—The annual club championship and open bicycle and flat races in connec- tion with this club are announced to take place on the ground of the St. Helens Cricket Club on the evening of Thursday next. Tne first prize offered for the 5 miles bicy- cle championship race (club) is a silver cup, to be won twice before becoming the property of the owner, and it is the present or the mayor (Alderman T. Cook). Along with it is given a gold medal, presented by the club. There are also second and third priz-s. The other events include a one mile bicycle race handicap and 100 yards flat race, and handsome prizes are offered in each. The sports are ap- proved by N C.A.A., and are under A.A. A. laws. A SERIES OF ASBAULTB.—At the Police Court, on Friday, Margaret Potter was charged with assaulting Alice Iligham, alias Lockhart, and the former issued a crone-sum- mons against the latter for a similar offence. The parties live in Grove-street. Mrs. Higham's allegation was that prisoner struck her three or four times on the face on Sun- day afternoon, and Mrs. Potter alleged that Mrs. Higham cournenced the assault. They were each bound over to keep the pease for three montbs.—A young man, named Thomas Jones, appeared to a summons charging, him with assaulting Eliza Lawrensoo, a married woman, who stated that defendant "abused her shameful!' Defendant, who said Mrs. Lawrenson struck him on the head with a bottle, was teed 103 and costs.—Mary Lawton, Parr-street, for as- saulting a neighbour named Jane Grine, by striking her on the month, splitting her lip, and loosening two teeth, was fined 2s fid and costs.

RESCUING A Pursomart.--john Brady, a rough- looking fellow, was brought up before Alderman Harrison and Mr. C. J. Bishop, at St. Helens, on Thursday, and charged with assaulting Police-constsble Cottam, in Liver- pool-street, en the 18,h March.—The Officer stated that he and Constables Hurst and Foxeroft had a man named M'Cormick in custody when prisoner and a man namnd Donoghue rushed up to his rescue. They kicked and struck the officers so violently that M'Cormick got away and the prisoner absconded. M'Carmick and Donoghue had been dealt with by the magistrates.—Superinteudent Johnston said prisoner had been convicted thirty-two times,' and he then held in his hand two commitments against the pri- soner.—He was committed for a month with hard labour, to follow two months on the commitments. Prisoner said he and the officer would have to meet sooner or later. DROWNING OASIS AT RAINFORD.—A distressing oc- currence took place at Rainford on Saturday last, resulting in the death of a boy named George Shuttleworth, 10 years of age, son of Mr. Ueorge Shuttleworth,. a collier, Orme- kirk-road, Rainford. It appeared that about two o'clock Shuttleworth, with two younger brothers and another lad named James Blinston, went playing together at an old un- used clay pit. Shuttleworth took off all his clothing with the exception of his shirt, and went wading into the water to drive off some ducks. After walking in Some distance he got out of his depth and shouted for assistance. Blinston ran for his mother, but when she arrived Shuttleworth was floadng face downwards in the water. With the assiptince of a man named Daniel Lee he was got out, but was quite dead. Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Bridge Inn, Rainford, on Whit-Monlay, when the jury returned a verdict of " Adidentilly drowned." &moor, ArrnxnANcE Coxstrrnn.,—On Wednesday afternoon, this committee held its canal meeting at the Town Hall. SIR S. NORTHCOTS AT Basusrox.—Sir Stafford North. cote, addressing an open-air ineering at Braunton on Wed- nesday night, reminded his audience of the approach of the general election consequent on the recent extension at the franchise, and, having stated that he should again•offer him- self as a candldare for North Devon, admonished his hearers to consider well how they would use the new privilege. He denied that he bad ever opposed the addition now made to the constituencies, and stated that the first great extension of the suffrage since the Reform Bill of 1832 was the Household Franchise introduced by Mr. Disraeli. He gave the history of the recent Bil 4-deprecating the attempt of the Government to postpone redistribution. He denied the Liberal party a monopoly of liberalism, and accused them of wanting to get rid of what the Conservatives desired to improve. He dealt also with the foreign policy of the Government which he condemned as involving the country in Woodshed and expenditure, which were abortive in re- sult and led to the disgrace of England in the eyes of the rest of the world, a policy which, he contended, offered a strong crintrast to that of the Conservatives. On Thursday, Sir Staff ird Northcote, continuing his Devonshire tour, addressed three meetings. He disposed of the charge that he told the same story over and over again by declaring that there was but one form in which the truth could be told, and asserting that his Radical opponents were in the habit of producing sensational effects by telling "good stout thumping lies." lie claimed that the Conservative party bad always been as anxious as their opponents to promote the welfare of the people, and that a large propor- tion of the legislation favourable to the working classes bad been originated by the party he represented. Whatever might be 'said of other measures, there could be no doubt, he said, that the Franchise and Redistribution Bills were the work of both parties. The tight hon. gentleman pro- ceeded to criticise the foreign policy of the Government, and expressed his surprise that a week after the Conserva- tive party acquiesced in ‘an almost unprecedented vote of credit the. Governmatt changed their policy. At one of the meetings the right hon. gentleman, after an allusion to the curiosity existing in connection with Lord Rosebery's visit to Berl* referred to the importance of India as a possession of the British Crown, and contended that a want of firmness on the part of our Government might forfeit the e,ontidence of the natives and imperil the British rule.

The overtime and-ni-g-t:t vv- --(lrk which had been relinquished La the Royal Arsehal has been ordered to be resumed for the manufacture of small arm ammunition, shot, and shell. Orders have also been issued t . expedite the armament and manning of reveral of the ocean steamers and mercan- tile fleet both at home and abroad as auxiliaries to the navy. The trample, t Cameo, which has just returned to Woolwich from Egypt with condemned and obsolete stores, had on Saturday partially diecherged her cargo when she received orders to cease unloading, and to ship with the utmost des- patch two hundred tons of compressed hay and proceed with it to Plymouth for the armed cruisers Oregon and Vancouver, ordered round to that port from Liverpool. The Cameo got away at seven o'clock on Saturday night. Until affairs between England and Buteia are definitely Settled the hired transports Egyptian Monarch, France, and City of Oxford, fitted to bring the troops from Egypt, Will not leave London, and no more troops will leave Egypt for the present. With the view of expediting the with- drawal of the British troops from the Nile stations to Alex- andria, forty or fifty iron lighters have been ordered of Lon- don ahipbui.dere. The Government will man the Cunard steamer Oregon with naval officers and sailors, the engineers being sup- plied by the owners of the vessels. The Government have also ached for a chief and second officer of the Cunard Company to accempany the vessel, which request will be granted. POILTSMOrTIT, MONDAX.—The transport Richmond Rill sailed this afternoon fur the Cape, with an immense amount of war materials, to, pedoes, and guncotton. She has the gunboats Tickler and Griper in tow. The transport Kimberley also galled, convoying the gunboat Gadfly to the game destination, Tun EXPERIMPLITAL eRrISR OH TIM BRITISH FLEET. The fleet which Admiral Hornby will command is to as- semble at Portland on June 6th. The object of the cruise upon which the fleet will proceed is to enable the Admiral to ascertain to the fullest extent the manoeuvring capabilities of the ships and their actual utility in case of war. For this purpose they will be in full fighting trim, and will be exercised in gunnery, and in torpedo warfare, ramming, and steam tactics. The principal operations will be carried on in Bantry Bav, but it is probable that the fleet may also Proceed to the Scotch coast. There will be altogether 20 shies, but several of these are practically of an obsolete type. It is, however, intended to be a fleet representing all classes of ships in the navy.

EXTRAORDINAB.Y ADVENTURE. —About four O'clock on Tuesday afternoon two weil-known local characters, named Jack Hewitt and Torn Sutton, went on the canal bank, behind Messrs. DiaHell's Foundry, St. Helens, to fight. Divesting themselves of everything but trousers, they fought several rounds, and their faces were beginning to present a very battsred aspect when intelligence of the encounter reached the ears of P.C.'s Hughes and Clarkson, who were on duty in the ne'ghbourhood. They proceeded behind the foundry wall, and sprang out within a few Yards of the combatants. Hewitt ran along the bank, but Sutton, who was apparently the more intox:cated of the two, sprang into the water and swain to the other side. Noticing, howe-er, that a number of persons had collected, and expecting that he would be held until the police got round, he refused to land. When the officers made a move he swam back again, and on Weir return he re-crossed. A young man named Rammer subsequently got ieto the water to assist Sutton, but he persistintly refused all aid. Even- tually he became exhausted, and when dragged out was in an unconscious state. P.. Callister, a certificated member (If the St' ic'ha Ambolapoe Association, had fortunately arrived, and he euccessfully used the ordinary means to re- store animation. An ambulance was afterwards procured. on which Sutton was conveyed to his lodgings irf Lyon. Street.

div.head: WARRINGTON BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON BUILDING SOCIETY.

The 15th annual meeting of the •Warrington Working- men's Permanent Benefit Bailding Society was held in Golborne-street schoolroom on Wednesday evening. There was a good attendance of members.—The MAYOR (Alder- man Harrison), who presided, said that in accepting the in- vitation to take the chair at that meeting he felt that he was identifying himself with an institution that was sound financially and, he believed, was an institution that had done a great deal of good, and one which, if all went well, would do a great deal more. There was nothing like ac- quiring habits of providence. We needed to be economical and judicious when we could, and to acquire the habit of saving, and institutions of that kind were sure to be a strong incentive. The managers, in their report, commenced by saying that they had pleasure in laying the financial report for the year tefore the members. He was sore that he shared that pleasure, and, if the managers had not pleasure in doing so it would not augur much for the substantial posi- tion of the society. But he thought that the managers, with very great credit to themselves, and without the slightest desire to exaggerate, might say that they had plea- sure in presenting their report. He had himself examined the balance sheet, and saw nothing that he could for a single moment call into question. He believed the society to be thoroughly sound, which was saying a good deal IR these days. The days of 15 per cent and 20 per cent seemed to have passed away, whether to return or not he could not say, but a building society ethat could clear its own, be in a sound position, and pay 4 per cent, was one upon which the sharehoders could very well congratulate themselves. They must hope that the good days of large dividends might again return. He then read the report, which was as follows :—" The sum of £1,299 3s. Id. has been received as subscrip- tions during the year, and £1,741 17s. 3d. for repayments, making the tool receipts £3,041 Os. 4d. The withdrawals during the year amount to £1,594 14s. 61. The sum of £1,300 has been sold to members during the year. There are 177 enb.ctibers holding 263± shares, and 30 borrowers holding 147.1 ehares, making a total of 213 members hold- ing 411 shares. The profits for the year, after deducting working expenses, amount to £297 17s. al., out of which the managers recommend a diaridend of 4 per cent., which will take £202 Is. 10d., leaving a balance of £35 15s. 44. to be carried forward to next yea' s account. The reserve fund amounts to £350, and the contingent fund to £5B 131.110." He (the chairman) thought that these statistics were very satisfactory.—Councillor DIXON moved the adoption of the report, and endorsed the remarks of the Mayor. Deprecia- tion of property, he said, had been great during the last 10 or 15 years, and although they could not have large divi- dends, many had had their misgivings relative to them—as to whether or not they were true ones.—Mr. HALL seconded the motion.—The CHAIRMAN read a letter from Mr. John Hough expressing satisfaction at the manner in which the business of the society had been conducted.—Mr. JAMES HARDING thought the report very gratifying. There was no doubt that of late years building societies had gone through a great crisis, and their society had gone through it very successfully, and had always had a balance in the bank.—The CHAIRMAN: I think the society has certainly outlived the attempt that was made to disparage it some years ago, and I think there can be no better proof of its good management and sound character.—lt was decided that a dividend of 4 per cent. be declared, on the motion of Councillor Dixon, seconded by Mr. JONES.— On the motion of Councillor Dtxotr, seconded by Mr. Lona- LAND, the following gentlemen were elected managers : Messrs. Harding, Wallington, Fenton, Taylor, Isherwood, and Rathborne.—Messrs. John Edward Wright and 'Thomas Dorriville were re-appointed surveyors, and Messrs. W. Ford and I. Leeson atsditors.—Mr. FENTON proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding. That society, he re- marked, made both ends meet, like a good house wife, in which way they save I"b ass." As showing the soundness of the society he mentioned that most of the property had been bought by men who lived in their own houses—work- log-men who purchased houses and paid the rent into the society, thee liquidating the debt.—Mr. HARDING seconded the resolution, and the trustees et the society were included in the motion—Mr. ISHERWOOD supported the proposition. Re remarked that the society did not lend money to specula- tors, and for that reason they did not get blocked with pro- perty. Speaking as agent to three or four societies he said that he could not turn to one except that one, which had never overdrawn its banking account —The vote of thanks was cordially passed and suitably acknowledged by the Mayor and by Mr. Hatton, who are both trustees. Tbe third trustee, Mr. C. 13. Barns. was not piesent —A Cordial vote of thanks to the secretary, Mr. Peter Dalton, con- cluded the proceedings.

Mr. Yates occupied the chair. The programme consisted of addresses, recitations, and music, and a very pleasant evening was spent. SUDDEN DBATH.—Charles Spencer, 55 years of age, em- ployed at Messrs. Mitchell, Arnott, and Co.'s paper staining works, Golborne, died suddenly last Friday. Deceased had been a work for some time owing to ill-health, but, feeling much better, he resumed duties again on Fliday at breakfast time. He had only been on the premises a few minutes, when he was taken suddenly ill, and had to 1:e removed home. His medical adviser was hastily summoned, but death ensued shortly afterNrards.

LIBERAL LECTURE. The first of a aeries of lectures organised by the Newton Liberal "300" was delivered In the Colborne Congrega- tional Schoolroom, on Friday evening, by the Rev. D. S. Prosser, of Walkden, on the subject : "Why should working men be Liberale?"'The chair was occupied by Mr. W. Mitchell, and there was a large attendance.—The Chairman reminded his audience that workingmen had now a voice in the ques- tion as to who should be members of Parliament, and that if they did not send the right men to the House of Com- mons it would be their own fault. He urged the claims of Colonel MeCorquodale upon the Gulborne electors, as against those of Sir R. Cross, because, he said, the latter be- longed to the party who had always gone in for class legis- lation to the neglect of the interests of the majority, the working me—Tho lecturer, in his address, styled Con- servatism as doing nothing at home and mischief abroad, and said that if the Conservatives had been in power at the present time their foreign policy of brag and bluster would inevitably have resulted in England being a't war with Russia. (Hear, hear.) One of the principal reasons why working men should be Liberals was that the Liberal party had conferred upon them the right of citizenship, notwith- standing prolonged opposition from the Conservatives. (Hear, hear.) The Liberals, he said, secured working men an inestimable boon in Free Trade, through which taxation was removed in a great measure from necessities and put on luxuries. The Liberals by removing the paper and stamp duties had provided the working man with his cheap news- paper. As to education, the working man had to thank the Liberals for placing his child in as good a position as the child of the rich possessed half a century ago. Religious liberty had been secured to them by the Liberals and work- ing men were now recognised as worthy of dignified posi- tions. As an instance the lecturer referred to working men having recently been placed on the magisterial bench, and assured his audience that the interests of working men would be protected in the future by the Liberal party, as they had been in the past. lie concluded by an appeal in favour of the candidature of Colonel McCorouodale.—The following resolution was passed unanimously :—" That this meeting considers Colonel McCown:dale a fit and proper person to represent the Newton Division in the new Parliament, end pledges itself to use all legitimate Elleitls to secure his return."—The usual votes of thanks were passed at the close,

div.head: TELEGRAPHIC BLUNDERS.
div.p: TELEGRAPHIC BLUNDERS.

A gentleman telegraphed from London to his brother in the country to send a hack to meet him at the station; but when the gentleman arrived at the station he found a sack waiting for him, A firm in London telegraphed, "Send rails ten foot lengths; " but the message was do livered, "Send tai/s in foot lengths." A person telegraphed to a friend to "take two stalls at the Haymarket ; " but the message conveyed directions to secure "two stables at the Haymarket." In another telegram, the intimation. "mother is no worse," was changed to "mother is or- snore." Again, "You will be glad to hear that your sister has accepted an engagement with your father's, approval," was rendered, that your sister has accepted an engagement with your father's apostle." In anothev case a plain business message, thus—" Come to me at early as you can, that we may arrange Wedne.day"—was given a matrimonial turn by being delivered as, "that we may arrange wedding." It has been left to America to produce a mistake in telegraphing which, while it is very amusing, could not result in hurt or disappointment to any one. Here it is,. just as received from the other side of the " ferry ": A St. Louis merchant, while in New York, received a telegram notifying that his wife was ill. He sent a message to his family doctor asking the nature of the sickness, and if there was any danger, and promptly received the answer: "No danger; your wife has had a child; if we can keep her from having another to•night she will do well." The mystification of the agitated busbard was not removed until a second inquiry revealed the fact that his indisposed lady had had a chill.—The Royal Mail. By James Wilson Hyde.

----------- His life is full of many stories. He has been engaged in many affairs of the heart. He is a man of warm reel- ing and much loyalty to those whom he loves; tempted to behave heartlessly, he has uniformly comported him- self honourably and well. He is to this day the mature child of a passion that is never unprincipled. He finds himself frequently in collision with the Parliamentary head of the army, the Secretary of State for Military Affairs, and with the high officials of the War Office, Lord Wolseley, and his men. He hears the vexati.ns which cross his path with equanimity, tempered or re- lieved by devotional ejaculations. The constitutional spirit which has become part of the Queen's nature and is as the breath of his nostrils to the Prince of Wales, dominates, in the main,, the Duke of Cambridge. He acquiesces, because the Constitution of the realm de- mands it, in much which he cordially detests. Yet if lie believes in his heart that the army, in consequence of new-fangled innovations, is goixt to the dogs or the devil, he never says so. Ile is, on the whole, a jovial optimist earl is rigtoieod e when he might have been a morose pessimist. He has the facility of his family for details. The dossier of every officer of any distinction in tmy he ar is at his fingers' ends. thel Tis Crimea, judgmentbuotf isnadn pt e i vei expert u tactics, lost his head how troops ought to be handled, whether at Aldershot or in the Soudan. He has an immense regard and an ex. i ee,e knw.l in e sirmated fear for public opinion— especially when that opinion finds articulate expression in print—and has be- fore now given excellent counsel, which ha sometimes been obeyed, to the Prince of Wales. Take him as he is, he is not only a favourable specimen of the home of Hanover, but a good specimen of a man.—Society tn London. By a Foreign Besident.

By J. Theodore Bent. , I= " HUNDREDWEIGIIT NUGGET" OF TASMANIA. ' The "Hundredweight Nugg.et " was found in July by an aboriginal servant of Dr. Kerr, about eight miles from that gentleman's head station, 53 miles from Bathurst. The gold was embedded in an isolated block of quartz, which was lying on the surface of the ground. The black. fellow, who had heard much ado about gold, saw the glittering treasure while he was rambling in the bush, and at once went home to acquaint his master, whereupon Dr. Kerr hurried back with the lucky discoverer. In the excitement of separating the gold from the quartz block in which it was encased, and which weighed about three cwt. in all, they unfortunately broke the lump into fragments. One lump was about a foot in diameter, and Weighed 751 b. gross, out of which 601 b. of pure gold was taken. The total weight of metal extracted was 1061 b. • Had it been preserved whole it would have been the largest lump of gold then found in the world, The black. fellow was rewarded by his master with two , Jocks of . sheep, two horses, a quantity of rations, and a team of bullocks to plough some ground for maize and potatoes.
