.• At Thursday's cession of the General Assembly of the Free Church of Scotland a resolution was passed affirming fist disestablishment was urgently demanded, and commit- ting the decision of the question to the people. Flak ON A baur.—A Lloyd's telegram from Stalham save :—The steamer Madge, from Yarmouth to Lynn, was h, ached on le 'near Eccles on Wednesday night. The ship is destroyed, but the crew, five in number, were landed at Paling. The origin of the fire is not yet ascertained. Auxins]) muumuu AT &A.—At North Shields, on Thurs- day. Attlaur Layton, chief officer of the NOVA Scotian brig- antine J. Williams, *as charged; in conjunction with the c•ptsin and second officer, with the murder on the high seas of Ugo Linninghan, under circumstances of alleged great brutality. The case was remanded for a week. ROYAL Von TO LZEDB.—The inhabitants of Leede have learned with eatistaction that their Royal Highnesses the Prince sod Princess of Wales will visit- the town for the Purpose of opening the new buildings of the Yorkshire College, on Wednesday, the 15th'July. Information to this effect was received from the Marquis of Ripon, the president of the College. MURDER OF A Mouten.—At an inquest on Thursday on , the body of the woman Ibrahim who was killed by her son at Buglawton a few days ago, it was stated that although sbe had been warned of the unsound mental condition of the young man the deceased had refused to allow him to be sent to an asylum. The jury returned a verdict of wilful mur- der against James Horabin. Tun haws Miwiternia.-11r..Gladetone attended early Communion service on Tuesday', at Hawarden, and until the afternoon was busy. with State affairs. About two o'clock oe took a brisk walk in the 'Palk and afterwards drove out. & large number of visitors, including the delegation of the Druids, some Americans from Ohio, and parties from Run- corn and towns in Lancashire, were disappointed by not .reing the Premier, who left the Rectory by. a private path; out they were admitted to view the ruins of the old castle end grounds. '1 XRRIBLE ACCIDENT.—A terrible accident has occurred et the Rose Mill, liollinwood,'near Oldham. Men were em- ployed In !tying iron girders along the floor of the top storey, when the girders npon which the platform jested gave way. Ten of the men fell to the gronati, a distance of eix storeys. Two were killed on the spot, two were so severely injured that recovery is not expeetedoind three others were also injured. . The mill was commenced about nine months since, and the brickwork appears to have given way. SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT LEIGIL—On Mon- day morning a shocking accident occarred at the Wood. end Colliery, Bedford Leigh, by which one man nettled Hugh Rielyard, lost his life. The deceased, with two feilow.workmen, was descending the pit, when the cage caught some obstruction, throwing the men oft their feet. The underlooker afterwards found the dead body of Rid. yard, shockingly mangled, at the bottom of the shaft. The Government Inspector was communicated with, and later in the day an examination of the mine was made. Tans BETTING RAID AT OLDHAM.—IMPORTANT LEGAL PourT.—At Oldham Police Coot, on Saturday, the hear- ing of the charges against William Mallalien, David Booth, Robert Clough, and Thomas Crabtree, for using and manag- ing the Bottom of Moor Cinb, kr the purpose of betting was rreumed.—lnspecter Purcer aad the Chief-Constable deposed to the apprehension of the prisoners, and the seizure of books, cards, dm., relating to horse racing, and upwards of £3O was found in the possession of the prisoners. —For the defence Mr. Cottinghara contended that it was a limited liability company, and that the prisoners did not contravene the Betting House Act by betting with members of the club. Even if the place were used for the purpose of betting, the "owners or occupiers" were an incorporated body, and the physical existence of that body was not before the court. Though they had got four• members of that company before them, they had not got the company itself, and the company mnst be taken all "the owners or oc- cupiers "of that OW. Be submitted it was not the in- tention of the Betting House Act to suppress such clubs, and in suppot t of his contention quoted a case decided byJus- tice Hawkins, who probably felt highly honoured at being at one time counsel for the Jockey Club. In conclusion, he said it was not necessary to refer to Tattereall's and other places, which were not touched, to show it was within the limits of the act of Parliament —The decision was adjourned to the 4th June when if necessary, liberty would be given to state'a case June, the Court of Queen's Bench. Sir,—The following is a schoolboy's version of the Arch- bishop of Canterbury's sermon at the " Varsity Church," Cambridge, last Sunday :—"The strmon was remarkable for its liberality; it was on foreign missions. He men- tioned the Wesleyan Missionary Society in the same cate- gory as the Church societies. Concluding, aftsr speaking of the ring of Sti.idd, Smithotc , &c to China, he used words somewh it to this effect—the change in the University to which at first we were firmly opposed may by mingling of the various creeds, and intercourse between various schools Of thought, lead to an ultimate reunion of the present divisions of sect, and promote in the highest degree reli- gious feeling in the University. He waP, of course, rear- ring to the admission of Dissenters. Suppose this kind of spirit made itself manifest amongst the parsons generally, and Warrington in particular, what a blessing it would bs to the community !—Yours truly, JOHN H. GORNALL.

div.head: FOOTBALL AT EARLESTOWN,
div.p: FOOTBALL AT EARLESTOWN,

- ---.--- - _ Sir,—l am an admirer of football, and nothing pleases me more than to see a bard-fough t game between two evenly balanced tearns,bot, Mr Editor,l have had my" sensibili ties" Shocked and my love for the game blunted and disgraced by the disorderly scenes that have been witneseed in Earles- town during the last two weeks. Football is, and should be, a manly and healthful exercise, but I am afraid it is rapidly developing into a brutal and demoralising " occupation," if what I have lately seen is any criterion. Ido not want to particularise any individual player or club, nor do I wish to condemn any one act or proceeding; but, sir, I think aome steps should be taken to put a stop to the disgraceful exhibitioos we have lately had. No doubt mach of what I complain about is due to the fact that the competing teams were local club-, but that is one more reason why the game Should be all the more pleasant and agreeable. Instead of there being a commendable rivalry between two local or- ganisations the end and aim of each one seems to be to damage the other as much as possible and injure the players in addition. This has been evidenced in matches on two following Saturdays, as many people in Earlestown know. Surely, when prominent members of one club urge the players to " Break his legs," Sic., what cars we expect but disturbance and dishonour in a football field? There is another evil I should like to draw attention to, and that is betting on the result of a match. This gives rice to many other evils, and this, too, should be put down with a strong hand. Trusting that my few remarks will tend to suppress the evils and nuisances I and others complain about, I am, yours, Arc., FOOThiLL. Earlestown, 27th May, 1885.

div.head: TUE BAND IN WARRINGTON PARK._
div.p: TUE BAND IN WARRINGTON PARK._

Sir,—Will you kindly find me a corner tEI whichto.say a word rempecting this pleasure-giving source. Music Is One of the highest and most elevating influences placed within the reach of the masses, and, as such, should be encouraged by all who care to see happy faces. I had the very great pleasure of listening to the band on the evening of Whit- Monday, and ae I stood and listened I could not help won- dering hew it wee all to be paid for. On this point I was enlightened before the evening pissed away. It seems that one gentleman has taken the trouble to gather around him a working-man's committee, whose duties are to see to the arrangements of the bands, mad to take some simple and enobtrnsive measures for coll Acting contributious. The duties of this committee should not be rendered too onerous by the stinginess of the public, and I hope the public will forgive me for using this word, as I am not quite sure that they deserve it. At all events it is either this or the mode of collecting contributions that is at fault, as on one even- ing the voluntary system felled to raise more than three- pence. It has never exc-eded three and sixpence, and yet the expenses can seldom be leas than nine shillings per even- ing. I believe its arranged for the band to play four evenings per week, and to pay each ?laver the large sum of 61 for his services. This will mean that the sum of 363 per week is needed. Now, where is it come from? The method now adopted of getting in contributions is faulty. I think the box should be pieced where everyone may see it, and yet never be surrounded hy a crowd. More than this, when the public kdow he true circumstances of the case, no doubt goineis will a m iuto the committee's exchequer. It must also be understood, to use my informant's words, himself one of the committee, "that they daresent play for nothing," so voluntaryism is now on its trial.—Yours, TRINT.

div.head: GORDON VERSUS BRADLAUGH.
div.p: GORDON VERSUS BRADLAUGH.

should think a considerable number of those who attended Mr. Bra llaugh's lecture in the Co-operative Hall must have, like myself, listened to him with mingled feel- ings. They could not but admire his power as a lecturer, and agree with a great deal that he said, but at the same time his remarks about General Gordon must have jerred upon them, and the way in which some of the audience seemed to endorse these remarks would be till more un- pleasant. The reason why Mr. Bradlaugh speaks adversely te General Gordon may, perhaps, not be far to seek. He is a popular lecturer with a reputation to maintain. TO de this he must above all things avoid the commonplace. Whatever else ke does he must tickle the intellectual pal- ates of his au,liences, and when he cannot do this with something that is sweet and soothing, he lets them have a Little of the astringent. He no doubt finds that next to being highly pleased. his auditors like to be gently shocked by hearing stated in a bold and unqualified way something that runs counter to the general feeling. Now, nothing. . . . is
more commonplace than praisa. of General Gordon. ,No

new sensation could be excited by "gilding refined gold," and therefore Mr. Bradltugh becomes depreciatory. Had it been as much the fashion to disparage Gordon as it is to praise him, Mr. Bradlaugh would very likely have been one of his most ardent defenders, and that for the same reason which now makes him a detractor. Mr. Bradlaugh' attacks can therefore be discounted, but when part of an audience, who are not at all affected by the exigencies of Popular lecturing, supports these attacks by their applause it is a different thing. I think those who did that must have derived all their knowledge of Gordon's character and career from Mr.Bradlaugh'e lecture. But even if we admit all that Mr. Bradlaugh said to be entirely correct, and that the deductions which ha evidently wished the audience to draw from what he said to be thoroughly justifiable. when we consider the eventful life which Gordon lived, and the strange scenes in avhich he enacted a prominent part, we cannot but wonder that so little that is serious can be said against him. It is, however, impossible to admit either of these suppositions. Mr. Bradlaugh's charges against Gordon amount to this— that he was mercenary and inhuman. To put them in this way is almost sufficient to disprove them. Gordon, be said, sold his services to the Chinese and the Khedive of Egypt, to fight in causes to which he was indifferent. Now, what are the facts with regard to China? The British Govern- ment was asked to appoint an officer to take charge of the Chinese Imperialist forces to cope against the Taeping rebels, and Gordon was selected for that post. The chief of the rebels against whom be was to fight is said to have com- mitted more crimes than any other human being, and his favourite amusement was to have his captives flayed alive or pounded to death in a mortar. As to Gordon's motives, let him Speak for himself. "I know," he says, "I shall Leave China as poor as I entered it, but with the knowledge that through my weak Instrumentality spwards of eighty to one hundred thousand lives have bean spared. I want no further eatiefaction than that." Instead of being animated by mercenary motives, he, when a sum of £lO,OOO was sent to him, divided the whole of it arriongst his troops. One thing he brought home with him was a valuable gold medal, which, having nothing else at the time to give, he anony- mously contributed to relieve those suffering from the cotton famine in Lancashire. The charges with regard to Egypt are equally baseless. What prompted Gordon's first and second journey to the Soudan was a desire to suppress the slave trade, and in- stead of taking the £lO,OOO a year offered to him as governor of that vast region, he would only accept £2OOO, which barely covered his expenses. Mr. Bradlaugh said Gordon had no love for the Soudanese, because he wished they had only one neck that he might break it. The whole char. acter of Mr. Bradlough's attack is summarised in this statement. What Gordon whiled was that the slave dealers, these who strew the caravan tracks of the Soudan with human bones, and perpetrate unheard of cruelties, bad but one neck that he might bre ,k it. And even this was but a mementary wish evoked by the horrors he so often wit- nessed, because he by no means broke the necks of all the slave dealers he had is his power. Gordon, Mr. Bradlaugh says, bought sieves and turned them into soldiers and this is one of his enormities which rack Mr. Bradlaugh's tender feelings. All I can say is that the last condition of these slaves was better than their first. Gordon, again, is accused ef distributing slave women amongst his soldiers as wives, whe scrambled for them. That certainly seems to be a startling application of the doctrines of free-love Mr. Bradlaugh is said to be theoretically if not practically enamoured of, but I certainly have not been able co find any account of it. Gordon mentions in one of his letters that in a division of slaves amongst some Arab tribes they "were not divided but scrambled"for," but I cannot suppose that Mr. Bradlaugh based' his statement upon that pass tge. Whatever may be the grounds Mr. Bradlaugh has for make log that ass.rtion, I feel oonvinced, taking into account the whole of Gerd, n's conduct, that the incident referred to Will bear an imerpretation vastly different to the interpre- tation he puts upon it. In conclusion, I shculd just like to advise those who seemed inclined to endorse Mr. Bradlaugh's attack on Gor- don's character to learn a little more of that officer's -doings, and I am convo.ce I they will-quickly begin to appreciate the literal exactness of Mr. Gladstone's words when he said that Gordon was a IKqo of heroes."

div.head: DEFENDER,
div.p: DEFENDER,

NEUTRAL NEWSPAPERS. Sir,—" Our neutral contemporary "—this is a phrase one frequently comes across, and it is generally quoted with a sarcastic allusion. It is hardly possible for an intelligent reader or writer to see or use the words without an accom- P inYin; snipe. Of all the antiquated things in existence, those papers which profess to be " neutral in all matters, political and religious." are the least deserving of respect— nay, one feels as if he ought to apologise for wasting paper and ink in calling attention to what ought simply to ha ig- nored. It is true not many now survive, and of the survivors as a rule it rn ry be said no harmless have they become that one cm sca-ceiy seriously advocate their disestablishment. We are more dispcsed to treat them as we treat the Chinaman to be seen at the entrance to certain tea establishments. What are commonly the c',aracteristics of such papers? To describe them as essentially time, dull, and insipid, would '

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: be te convey barely half the truth. They lack boldness, in- dependence, and originally; being in fact the most Colour. less, flavourless, milk-and-watery productions, that somehow mange to pass muster in this age of marvellously cheap and

good newspaper literature. It is human nature to take sides in witnessing a contest, a race, or even a prize-fight; equally so in politics. There roust therefore appear to proprietors and publishers of news- papers which proclaim their neutrality good and sufficient reason for the course they adopt. If we try to risad their motives it is probable we shall come to the conclusion that they are pretty much the same as actuated the man with the donkey; and observation tells us they usually achieve about- the same amount of success. Afraid of giving offence by a frank and honest expression of opinion and a bold and fear- , less championship of what they conceive to be the right, they go on their hum-drum way, ridiculed by some, ignored by most, and earning the genuine respect of few whose res- pect is worth baying. Toere is another feature common to most publications of this class, which tends to lower them in popular esteem. " Things are not what they seem," says the poet. Neither are the so-celled neutral newspipers what they profess to be. Under the guise of neutrality, the majority lean percep- tibly to Conservatim, and indeed covertly advocate Conser- vative principles. This as4ertion is cipable of proof, and will not be disputed by observant newspiper readers. An open opponent who shows his colours, and strikes fairly above the belt, commands our respect, and we meet him gladly as foeman worthy of our steel. On the other hand, coward is the fittest epithet we can apply to him who, lack- ing the courage to join the ranks on either side, miss no opportunity from behind the banner of neutrality of giving a stab in the dark ta the party he secretly dialikes. If neu- trality men dare do no more, they assiduously extol the virtues of their favourites, and expose the failings of the party they in their heart of hearts fervently hate; and this too, be it observed, not by cleverly written original articles, but by copious quotations gleaned from a wide field. This tactic is on' largely employed, being evidently considered an easy and safe, if not strictly honourable, mode of war- fare. As out and out Tory or a red hot Radical, whether in , man or newspaper, is infinitely to be preferred to one wearing the garb of neutrality.—Yours, *c., A. C.

div.head: IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.
div.p: THE IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.

Sir,—With your permission I wish to say a few words to Mr. O'Brien. Ido not doubt his great and overwhelming anxiety to perpetuate the system that makes it possible for all Irishmen to feel " proud" that the "same good gracious Queen, Lords and Commons," may continue ta rule over Ireland. The only thing I doubt is as to whether the ma- jnrity of his countrymen are of the same mind ; if they are, well, the least I can say is, they have a strange way of showing it. But, suppose we deal with a few facts, and suppose, also, that I ask Mr. O'Brien to eschew impudence, and take to argument, and we shall get on better. Now, what do we find ? Why, this: that the several quotations I have already given from speeches of prominent Irish speakers are quietly ignored by "Chairman" and by Mr. O'Brien. If I cared very much for the success of the Liberal party, I should quietly accept the position here taken up, feeling, that Warrington Irishmen being ashamed of their speakers, wished all to be forgotten and forgiven; but knowing, as I do, that the two political parties are just now subject to a force they cannot resist, and must soon take new shape and form, I am anxious that out of chaos residents of the British Isles shall receive permanent and lasting laz nefit. I- accept Mr. O'Brien's position with great plea- sure, viz., that the late Mr. Isaac Butt's programme is all that Irishmen want, and that the word "separation" has only been drawn into the speeches of Irishmen, as witness the speech of Mr. Cox recently de- livered at Warrington. by their well-known relish for any- thing hunaourous or playful. It may he that Mr. Biggar was only joking when he said " they" (the Irishmen) "hated England," and that when speaking of the Conserva- tive candidate and Mr. MoMinnies he was not truthful when he said "They both hated Ireland, and did all they coald against it." Yet if this was Irish humour it gives one a creepy feeling that is not quite pleasant. Perhaps Mr. O'Brien will favour your readers with his opinion upon this point, and will also tell us what was meant when Mr.Biggar said "So that in the end probably England would be con- fined to the one island which was at present called Great Britain. (Laughter.)" Does Mr. O'Brien's interpretation of this passage lead him to believe in Mr. Biggar's loyalty to "our gracious good Queen?" When at Killrnallock the Irish people called out "Three cheers for the Mandi " was it the bursting forth of their pent up loyalty towards Her Majesty, who in her trips to the continent and during her long sojourns among the canny Scot?, leaves her dear Irish subjects to the mild and beneflcient sway of Dublin Castle? Previous to leaving this portion of the subject allow me to notice, by a few words, the presence of Mr. T. P. O'Con- nor, M.P., at Widnes. The Chairman, Dr. O'Keeffe, was kind enough to make reference to the Warrington police and their conduct at the recent meeting. He said—" The Inspector knew the people of Widnes were able to conduct themselves in such an excellent manner that there was no occasion for the introduction of detectives amongst them, or for the abominable espionage, which was so detestab'e in itself." By implication I read this to mean that the War- rington police would have taken the same course had they have had the same confidence in the Warrington Irishmen; not having this confidence they attended the meeting, when the want of "excellent conduct" on the part of tbe con- veners of the meeting caused, to use the words of Mr. Loughlin, "the meeting to be broken up." I say distinctly Dr. O'Keeffe makes a distinct charge of misconduct against the Warrington branch of the Irish National League, and justifies the conduct of Chid Constable, Mr. Haut, and his detectives." This is a great pity; all meetings should and must be of such a character as to challenge at any time the presence of 1 rePresentatives of the law. If conducted otherwise, they give ground for suspicion, and, under present circumstances, are liable to occasional visits from the police. Now as to Ireland, I may not know as much of Irish history as Mr. O'Brien, but I assure him that what little I do know is of a very sad nature. So sad indeed that it has led me to urge on the platform and in the Press the great and dire necessity that exists for more humane and less coercive measures in our dealings with Ireland. Mr. O'Connor, in his speech at Widnes, said 'The Parliamen- tary representatives of the country (Ireland) had been rotten." If we were to direct our studieo in this direction we should be woefully convinced of its truth, and lam sadly fraid the term, strong as it is, is equally applicable to-day to some of these who aim at leading the people to acknowledge and crown C. S. Parnell king of Ireland." In 1761 the same oppressive and unjust landlordism that to-day we witness in Skye was working out its evil objects in Ireland. The Levellers of the White-boys arose, and to put down tithe-mongers and avaricious landlords, the first of what has been a series of secret societies, was originated. Going about the country, they forced the people to swear to be true to them, yet the first five that were executed solemnly declared that "it never entered into their thoughts to do anything against the King or the Government." The cry of Catholic rebellion was raised by the landlords, and if Mr. O'Brien will read Sister Clare's history of Ireland he will find that they had already made to their hands each a complete code of Penal Laws as quite justified Sidney i Smith in saying "Such jobbing, such profligacy, so much direct tyranny and oppression, such an abuse of God's gifts, such a profanation of God's name for the purposes of i bigotry and party spirit, cannot be exceeded in civilised Europe, and will long remain a monument of infamy and shame to England." This state of things existed when Ire- land boasted of an Irish Parliament. Mr. Ogle, speaking ! in the Irish House of Commons, said "The landed man is the great extortioner. There is hardly an estate which is not let to the highest penny and much above its value." All this happened when Ireland had, after a fashion, Home Rule. From this time it would be easy to trace the history of the various secret societies, and I may say it is in this direction that we must look for the true history of Ireland. Take the history of Orangeism as displayed in Ireland. I have before me now such ruthless and heartrending sketches elf their high-handed dealings with their Catholic neigh- bours that are enough to stifle all hope, but want of room will not allow this question to be touched. Since November, 1873, when Mr. Isaac Butt formulated the Home Rule programme, we have seen the I. La cause, chatnelion-like, change its colour day by day, and we now request a plain and definite statement of their objects, so that we may know how far Englishmen nsay co-operate with them for the achievement of that object. In spite of the charge of "rottenness" made by Mr:O'Connor, one cannot think of the stirring times of Emmett, Fenton, Lalor, and a host of other true-hearted Irishmen without hoping that Ireland has still true sons, men who, guided by the experi- ences of the past, will avoid the rocks upon which past enterprises have struck, and will recognise the value or ' steady, yet persistent courses for the regeneration 01 Ireland. May 25, 1835.

It is believed in naval circles that during the cruise of the Evolutionary Squadron, Admiral Hornby will have sealed orders for a foreign station, so as to be prepared for any eventualities. In making his escape the thief knocked a woman down and dropped a bag containing DM LIBERAI LECTURE.—In the Co-operative Hall, Earles- town, on 'Monday evening, the second of a series of lectures to be delivered throughout the Newton division, under the auspices of the Liberal Council of the "300," was given by the Rev. D. S. Prosser, of Walkden. There was a large 1 audience. Mr. T. Howard (Earle-street) presided. Tne subject was "How will the new electors vote P " and the theme was ably handled. Liberalism, it was argued, had a claim upon both the interest and the support of the work- ingman, and the boons granted in the past by the Liberal Dirty would be excelled in their future legislation. Amongst future reforms might be expected the temperance ques- tion, and the impor's-et business of local government In 1 conclusion the leqtarer urged Isis audience to show their ap- preciation of the working-man's vote by using it itthearty support of Ike Government at the general election. The Chairman remarked that their candidate (Colonel McCor- qaodale) was so far in favour of working-men becoming members of Parliament that he had subscribed to the ex- penses of the working-men's candidate for the Hindley divi- sion. (Loud applause.) The usual votes of thanks con- eluded a hearty meeting.

SUDDEN DEATlL—William Lawton, a man of about 60 years of age, who kept a small general dealer's shop in Dial-street, died suddenly on Wed- nesday morning in an out-building connected with his premises. A neighbour who heard him groan- ing, and went to him, found him dying. Deceased :had been ailing for sometime past. A certificate of death was given, so that an inquest was not neces- sary.

--- • GR A.PPENH AL te. 1 Last evening a public meeting of the Conservatives, elec- tors and non-electors, residing in Grappenhall, Knutsford Division. was held in the large room at Grappenhall, to transact political business, and hear an address from the Hun. Tatton Egerton, M.P., ConservaLve candidate for the Knutsford Division. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Chant n Parr, and arnengst those also present were the Hon. Tatton Egerton, M.P., the Rev. Canon Greenall, Major Litton, and Messrs. John White, E. J. Nicholson, Edward Greenall, Tinsley, Joseph Cliffe, H. J. Longton, John Pim- lott, and Lance Bentley (principal agent), dm., eltc. Teere was not a very large attendance.—The CHAIRMAN said that it would be sufficiently evident to all who bed studied the course of events for some time past that in consequence of the Franchise and Redistribution Bills, now virtually pesiel, the whole of their hitherto existing management would have to be altered, and for that reason the meetieg had been called, so that they could consider business matters regard- lag that district.—Mr. L. BENTLEY, the agent, in explaining the object of the meeting, said that the alterations heing made seriously affected the county of Chester. Although in the past they had three constituencies who returned eight members, they would have 8 constituencies etch returning one member, but in those eight constituencies, it was be- lieved, the voting strength would be quite as great as all the three now existing, so that although the new diviiion of Knut-lord had been created out of a portion of old Mid- Cheshire and old East Cheshire, and now con- tained only about 2,000 voters, the altered state of affairs under the new register would add something like 10,000 to it. The Krmtsford division was perhaps one of the most extraordinery in Cheshire. It extended from near Wirrington to very near Buxton, and while in the whole of that area there were only abeut 53,000 people, from that number they would in future have as many electors as there were formerly in the whole of the constituencies of Mid-Cheshire. This enormous increase came from a class that has not hitherto exercised the fran- chise, and that was one of the reasons that had made it necessary to hold those meetings, to organise the party, and give the electors the opportunity of taking part in anything concerning the welfare of the party in that division. The Central Committee, he went on to explain, was formed so as to give every township in the envision at least one representative, the numbers being based on the population. Appleton, with a population of 2,067, would return 11 representatives; Cowley, popula- tion 200, 1; Grappenhall, population 788, 4. Latchford would return 12 represent stives.—Businese was then pro- ceeded with. Mr. C. Parr was elected chairmen of the "Grappenhall polling division, representatives were appointed on the Central and Executive Committees, and a District Committee was formed —The Hon. Tatton Egerton after- wards gave an address.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

CONSERVATISM AT FRODSHAM.-011 Monday N 0.2 Branch of the Everton Working-men's Conservative Association held their second annual pic-nic at the Overton Hills, Frod- sham. The meeting was a most succe3sful one, there being ever )50 persons present, and a very enjoyable afternoon was spent. It a Meeting held on the grounds Mr. JoneS, , the chairman, commented upon the succesiful gathering ' that had been held, and asked Mr. Councillor Houlding to say a few words to the meeting.—Mr. lioulding thanked the electors of Everton for the manner in which they had worked to secure his election.—Dr. Flinn proposed a resolu- tion condemnatory of the policy of her Majesty's Govern- ment at home and abroad, which was seconded by Mr. Mar- tin. and carried unanimousiy. NARROW ESCAPE AT FRODSHAM STATION.-011 Wednes- day night, Mr. Thomas C. Williams, insurance agent, of Runcorn, had a narrow escape at the Frodsham Railway Station. The platform was crowded with passengers await- ing the arrival of the train for Runcorn. As the train en- tered the station a passenger opened a door and carelessly allowed it to swing backwards and forwards, to the immi- nent peril of persons standing near the edge of the platform. As the carriage passed, Mr. Williams seized the handle with the intention of fastening the door. He, however, failed to carry out his object, and fell heavily upon the footboards, where he lay, and might at any moment have fallen under the wheels of the train. Much excitement prevailed, and Mr. Williams was congratulated upon so fortunately escap- ing from serious injury. ERODSHAM MEN CHARGED WITH FRIO:M.—AA Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, William Wynne and John Dimelow, both of Frodsham, were charged with having on the 26th inst. travelled from Liverpool to Runcorn on the London and North-Western Railway without having previ- ously paid their fare, with intent to defraud the company. It appeared the prisoners alighted from the last train on the previous night, and when asked for their tickets explained that they had formed two of a pic-nic party, and the person who had the tickets had gone on by a previous train. As they had no money to pay the fare, the prisoners were taken into custody.—The prisoners stated that they had no intention to defraud the company, and that if the case were adjourned they would prove the truth of the assertion. —The case was adjourned, the prisoners being admitted to bail.

SEIZURE OF UNWHOLESOME MEAT.—At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Rupert Saunders, cork butcher, of Fredsham, was summoned for, on the 17th of April, at Frodsham, having in his possession 27 pieces of meat, for the purpose of preparation for sale and intended for the food of man, the same being unsound; unwholesome, and unfit for human consumption.—Mr. Linaker, solicitor, of Frod- sham, appeared on behalf of the Runcorn Rural Sinitary Authority, and Mr. Dreaper. of Chester, defended.—Mr. Joseph Farrington, the inspector of nuisances to the Run- corn Rural Sanitary Authority, said that on the 17th of Apil be visited the defendant's premises at 8-45 pm. Saunders was away from home. He saw Mrs. Saunders and the servant. He found, in the store room, the pieces of meat enumerated in the information. He considered them unwholesome, and he took them from the premises and put them In a stable, at an hotil. He did not think the place where he found them should contain such meat, as they made sausages and pies there. He took the first train from Preston Brook Station on the follow- ing morning, and went and informed the medical officer, Dr. Joseph Adams, of Warrington, of the occurrence.— Dr. Adams said he examined the meat spec fled in the in- formation. A number of renderings of lard were carefully kept apart from anything else. They were stale but not actually smelling, as were some of the other things. There was a large amount of suet and fat put together, and that wag in the condition of partial putrefaction, with a little green mould on parts of it, and was not fit for human con- suniption.—Mr. Dreaper then addressed the Bench for the defence —Sarah Absworth said she was in the employ of the defendant. She had seen similar accumulations of food put into the wash tub and given to her brother for his pigs. She heard the defendant say he was going to keep pigs and use up the stuff. They never used any bad meat for mak- ing sansiges.—William Booth, commimion agent, Fred- sham, said defendant came to him about a fortnight before the seizure of the meat, and asked him if he could sell him a pig-cote. Witness said he could not, and subs:fluently defendant asked him if be would allow him to use his pig- locite until he (defendant) bad one ready, and he consented. , —After about five minutes' deliberation, the Chairman said : Tbe Bench feel it is their duty to convict in a pen- alty of £lO and ICls 6d costs.—Mr. Dreaper asked to be allowed to state a case, but this the magistrates re- fused.

• WHITSUNTIDE AT FRODSHAW—The usual demonstration of the Friendly Societies took place at Frodsham on Whit- Monday, but the event has for some years been declining in importance, as the number of clubs and members wino walk is considerably reduced, and the same interest does not ; appear to be taken by the rnemhers in displaying the regalia of the societies. On Monday the Ancient Foresters of Court Independence, No. 410, were the first to make a start in procession for church, headed by the Frodsham Amateur Brass Band, and out of 257 members 41 attended. This club ' has dispensed during the past year in sick and funeral allow- ances £332 2s 6d, and its funds on the 31st December, 1884, ' amounted to £2,643 lie 4d. The Modern Druids Society, , headed by the Ellesmere Port Brass Band, mustered 33 out of a total of 77 members, and from the annual statement of • accounts, has expended £ll2 15s id in sick pay and for funerals during the year, the money in hand at the close of the year being £302 Os ed. The Odd fellows Club was headed by the Church Bible Class Brass Band, which naade its first • appearance in public, and came in for a good share of Praise for its efficiency. Tbia club is a strong one, but through some misunderstanding was not well represented, as only 19 members appeared in the procession. The Na- tional Anthem was played by each band on arriving at the south door of the Parish Church. The Bev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar, conducted the servl.ce, assisted by the Rev. A. Butler, curate, which consisted of the Communion Service and the Epistle and Gospel for the day. The Vicar preached from James i., 22, " Be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only." After the service the clubs made their annual visit to their patrons, and the weather beim; beauti- fully fine, a large number of people assembled at the Park to watch the arrival of the clubs, and listen to the bands discoursing their choicest pieces on the lawn. The whole of the Park grounds were thrown open to the public by Mr. Wright during the visit of the clubs, and the privilege was very much appreciated by the visitors. The peach-house, conservatories, American ground, and the geometrical flower garden also received deserved attention and admiration. In the evening the standings, swing boats, hobby-horses, and &her accessories to the fun of the fair, which had been fixed in the main street, were extensively patronised. Over- ton Hills were the scene of festive gaiety, hundreds of visi- tors from the neighbouring towns having sought the spot io search el the amusements provided, and to inhale the , bracing breezes, and enjoy the view of river, wood, and plain presented.

COLLISION AND Loss OF TWENTT•TWO LivEs.—The City of Rome, which arrived at New York on Thursday morn- ing, reports that when 25 miles off tbe Banks, at half-past four in the afternoon, during a fog, she struck the fishing batquo George John, which was ridirlg at anchor. The bar- que tank immediately, and 22 of lira crew were drowned.
I LATEST NEWS.
Sir Charl.m Duke left Dublin on Friday morning for London. Lord Resebery arrived at Dover by the CalaL boat on Friday morning, and left by the express for London at 4.15 a.m
At Hull, on Friday, a seaman named Womack was fined £lOO and costs for destroying smuggled tobacco after it had been Seized,

Lord Salisbury journeyed from Hatfield to London en Friday morning, returning in the afternoon after attending the funeral of the Dowager Countess of Galloway. The semi-official journal St. Petersburg publishes 'a itb- out comment an article which recently appeared in the Memorial Diplomatigue, urging the necessity of restoring Ismail Pacha to the throne of Egypt, A BOY BILLED.—A boy named Gorden, aged five years, residing in James-street, Aberdeen, was run over by the horse of a tramway car in St. Nicholas, Aberdeen, on Friday foramor. The wheels of the car passed over his chest, and he died shortly afterwards.

A Sr:mm.363lmm EOl2-0-WNED.—Early on Friday. morning William Dickin, platelayer, of Willenhall, got up from bed and walked out of the house. He was found lying dead in an old swag full of water only a few yards away from his own door. It is believed that the deceased walked into the water in his sleep. THE DUTIES ON WINES.—At a meeting of Colonial mer- chants and others interested in the wine trade of the colo- nies, held on Friday at the London offices of the Agent- General for Cape Colony, a resolution was unanimously passed calling upon the Government to adhere to their pro- posals modifying the duties on wines notwithstanding the failure of the commercial negotiations with Spain. TERRIBLE FALL WHILE BIRDNESTING —On Thursday evening Dr. Churton held an inquest at Helsby on the body of Heim Edith Parker, daughter of a butcher. The child, with her brothers and sisters, went up to the highest point of Helsby Hills birdnesting. She saw a nest beneath, and was clambering down when she slipped and fell, bounding from rock to rock. She was picked up inseneible, and died without recovering consciousness. A verdict of accidental death Was returned. THE SHOCKING MATRICIDE IN CHESHIRE.—At Congleton on Friday morning, James Horabin, a young farmer, was charged with the wilful murder of his mother. The prisoner, who was in the custody of two police officers, ap- peared with his throat bandaged. The police applied for a remand. It appears that the prisoner was courting a young widow worms at Huelawton, and that his mother was bit- terly opposed to the prospective union, and frequent quar- rels resulted. Mrs. Horabin owned the farm on which she lived, and but for this terrlble tragedy the prisoner would also have come into possession ef zaooo on her death. The night prior to his fatal attack upon his mother the prisoner rushed upon his uncle and attacked him in a dread- ful manner with a mallet, but was evrntuelly beaten off. The prisoner cried bitterly when he saw the wounds inflicted by his knife. He was remanded.

MILITARY PREPARATIONS. Orders were received at Sheerness on Friday directing the crew of blue jackets ta be immediately selected for H M.S. Leam'er, commissioned in the Medway for particular ser- vice. The Leander is a new fast war cruiser, equipped with ten six-inch steel breech-loading guns, and twelve Nordenfeldt's and Gatling machine guns, besides spar tor- pedoes. Her destination is unknown, but it is believed he will join the Evolutionary Squadron under Admiral Hornby. Ths corvette Rover, fourteen guns, was placed upon the active list, being now in readiness for immediate service.
THE EVACUATION OF THE SOUDAN. CAIRO. FRIDAY.—The force under General Comer cnm- pletely evacuated Tarnai yesterday morning. AltogEther 6,000 refugees have now left Dongola for Lower Egypt.

--- A Central News telegram dated Suakim, Friday morn- ing, states :—The small portion of the Suakin' Berber Rail- way, which has been laid, is now being worked entirely by Royal Engineers, and no further metals are being laid. All the navvies brought here by Messrs. Lucas and /lyre have now left, and many of the transports are clearing out of the harbour. Sickness :Is on the, increase among the troops remaining here. SIJAHI3I, FRIDAY.—The percentage of sickness amongst the troops here is 69, which compares ve,y favourably with the state of affairs at Massowah, where the Italian garrison is being almost decimated by disease.
